chapters.title: Council Staff gives procedural instructions for the hearing

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: For the hearing on cultural affairs, libraries, and international relations, you are in the right place.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify, please fill out a witness slip.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: They can be located outside.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You walk past the desk when you walked in.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Once again, if you're here to testify, please fill out a witness slip.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you need any assistance, you could seek a sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, there's no eating or drinking in the room.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Once again, no food or beverages inside the room.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At no time is anyone to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We thank you for your kind cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Y a poco no se va.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Maybe he was not here.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning once again folks.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you're here for the hearing on cultural affairs, libraries, and international relations, you are in the right place.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify, please go outside and receive a witness slip.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Fill that out, you can give it to one of the sergeant at arms.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams welcomes attendees to the oversight hearing 'Telling Our Stories: Examining the Research Collections of New York City's Public Libraries.' She introduces herself as Chair of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations.
chapters.title: Chair Williams opens hearing on research collections

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's so nice to see them outside of City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Nantosha Williams, Chair of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Welcome to our oversight hearing, telling our stories, examining the research collections of New York City's public libraries.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams announces the four resolutions to be heard: Res 27 on purchase of claims, Res 28 on ending the Financial Oversight Board, Res 372 on repealing Act 22, and Res 494 on stopping Project Esencia. She notes the serendipity of hearing them at the Schomburg Center.
chapters.title: Chair Williams introduces four Puerto Rico resolutions

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In addition to our oversight topic today, we will be hearing the following legislation.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I said this at the press conference that it's really serendipitous and there's so much alignment in us hearing these resolutions because we didn't plan to hear them here, but this is the perfect place.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we will be hearing resolution number 27 sponsored by Councilmember Alexa Aviles calling upon the New York State Legislature to pass

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and the governor to sign legislation in relations to the purchase of claims by corporations or collection agencies and to certain instruments calling for payment of a monetary obligation by a foreign state.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Resolution number 28, also sponsored by Councilmember Aviles, calling on the United States Congress to establish a date certain for ending the Financial Oversight and Management Board of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Resolution number 372, sponsored by Councilmember Justin Sanchez, calling on the Legislative Assembly of Puerto Rico to pass and the Governor of Puerto Rico to sign legislation to repeal Act 22.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and implement a progressive tax policy to minimize the revenue losses to federal, state, city, and territorial governments,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and Resolution 494, also sponsored by Councilmember Aviles, standing with the people of Puerto Rico to stop the construction of Project Asensia, a luxury development in Cabo Rojo.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams explains that the Schomburg Center is named for Arturo Schomburg, a Puerto Rican writer and activist who amassed a collection of 10,000 items. She notes the center now holds over 11 million items preserving Black history and culture.
chapters.title: Chair Williams connects hearing to Schomburg Center and Arturo Schomburg

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It is fitting that we are hearing these resolutions today, sitting in the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, which was named for Arturo Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Schomburg was actually born in Puerto Rico to a Puerto Rican father of German descent and an Afro-Caribbean mother from the Danish West Indies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: He immigrated to New York City when he was just 17.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: A writer, historian, curator, and activist, Schomburg amassed an extraordinary collection of 10,000 items that spoke to the intellectual,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: artistic, and cultural legacies of Africans and individuals of African descent.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Some of those items are still housed right here today among the over 11 million items that preserve an important part of local, national, and global Black history, arts, and culture.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They helped to make the Schomburg Center the preeminent institution of its kind worldwide.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We will hear more about the resolutions in a minute.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams reads from and discusses the book 'There Was a Party for Langston' by Jason Reynolds, illustrated by Jerome and Jared Pumphrey. She connects it to the Schomburg Center's role in preserving the works of Langston Hughes and other Black writers.
chapters.title: Chair Williams discusses book 'There Was a Party for Langston'

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But first, a few words about our oversight topic, which also honors the recent 100th anniversary of the Schomburg Center.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I have this book.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, it's a library.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You can clap for books.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So a staff member happened upon this beautiful book, lovingly written by best-selling and award-winning author Jason Reynolds and brilliantly illustrated by acclaimed brothers Jerome and Jared Pumphrey.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It is titled, There Was a Party for Langston, King of Letters.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The cover page illustration shows a stream of party goers entering the Schomburg Center of the New York Public Library just as you entered today for our hearing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The first page goes like this.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: There was a party for Langston at the library, a jam in Harlem to celebrate the word-making man.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Here are the party goers entering the Langston Hughes Auditorium at its grand opening in February 1991, just as you entered for our hearing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So today is not exactly a party for Langston Hughes, but it is a recognition and examination of the work our city's libraries do to preserve and present his poems

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and his stories and his nonfiction works and the poems and stories and nonfiction works of so many other writers shown here.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And there's so many people.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I was like amazed at this book.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So from James Baldwin to W.E.B.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Du Bois to Count T.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Collins to Claude McKay to Zora Neale Hurston, Alice Walker, Toni Morrison, Gwendolyn Brooks, Richard Wright, and more.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It is also a recognition and examination of the work being done every day at the Schomburg Center for the past 100 years.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams describes the research collections of the New York Public Library, Brooklyn Public Library's Center for Brooklyn History, and Queens Public Library's Black Heritage Reference Center. She highlights the staff and funding required to support these collections.
chapters.title: Chair Williams outlines research collections across three library systems

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But our hearing today also goes well beyond the Schomburg Center to bring attention to the research collections of all three of our public library systems.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Those collections include the New York Public Library for Performing Arts, Dorothy and Louis B.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cullum Center, and the research divisions in Center's House and New York Public Library's flagship Stephen A.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Swartzman Building, the Brooklyn Public Library's Center for Brooklyn History, Center for Brooklyn History,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Originally founded as the Long Island Historical Society in 1863 and now residing in an 1881 Brooklyn Heights building, much of which has been designated as an interior landmark by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And the Queensborough Public Library's Carter G.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Woodson Reference Collection of African American Culture and Life, as well as the Queens Public Library's Black Heritage Reference Center located in Corona

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: at the Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center, which was the first public building to be named for the Harlem Renaissance literary giant.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Who had died in 1967, just two years before the library was founded.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks an anonymous donor for a $60 million gift to the NYPL for the Performing Arts. She emphasizes the committee's role in examining how libraries manage public trust and resources.
chapters.title: Chair Williams thanks donor and discusses public trust

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The committee knows that it takes a lot of staff and money to support these remarkable collections, and we should discuss that today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Personally, I want to thank the anonymous donor who just contributed $60 million to the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: which will go towards digitizing, preserving, and cataloging its 15 million item archives so that even more interested patrons here and abroad can access it well into the future.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As a staff member at the Center for Brooklyn History told committee staff, it is our job as librarians to preserve these documents and artifacts forever.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Given the enormity and importance of that work and the amount of money, including public money, that it takes to do it well, the committee is also cognizant of the fact that our city's libraries are in a position of extraordinary public trust

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and that their work should be examined carefully.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams notes this is the first off-site City Council hearing since COVID. She shares her mother's Harlem roots and highlights the Schomburg Center's 100th anniversary and its historic significance.
chapters.title: Chair Williams shares personal connection to Harlem and Schomburg

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Finally, I hope this is finally, let me say that it is our great pleasure to be here at the Schomburg Center in the village of Harlem, as they say.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I said that right?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I have to say, fun fact, my mom was raised in Harlem and seen Harlem in the Bronx, even though I'm a Queens girl.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: This is our first off-site hearing, which we have not done as a city council since COVID struck our city.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We are especially honored to be just steps from Langston Hughes'lobby with his Rivers Art installation commemorating Hughes'well-known poem, The Negro Speaks of Rivers, and under which Hughes'ashes are interred.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We are thrilled to be so close to the reading room where original and memorable paintings of Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas hang overhead into the historic American Negro theater.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: which launched the careers of Harry Belafonte, Sidney Poitier, Ruby Dee, and other acclaimed black actors.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Happy 100 years to this great institution and to its staff members who keep it running for benefit of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: May you all have 100 more.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Now let me invite Councilmember Aviles to speak about her resolutions.

chapters.summary: Council Member Alexa Aviles thanks the committee and introduces the four resolutions on Puerto Rico. She connects the hearing to Arturo Schomburg's legacy of fighting for Puerto Rican and Cuban independence.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles introduces Puerto Rico resolutions

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Buenos días.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker Williams and the members of this committee and everyone here from New York City and Puerto Rico who have joined us for this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Today the committee is considering four resolutions on the future of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: The self-determination of the island's people.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Resolution 27, 28, 494, and 372.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: It is befitting that we are hearing these resolutions today at the Schomburg Center.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: As the Deputy Speaker mentioned, Arturo Alfonso Schomburg was a black Puerto Rican activist who was deeply committed to Puerto Rican and Cuban independence.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: He believed in a future free from colonial rule and self-determination of all people.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: That fight for freedom and self-determination

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: continues in Puerto Rico.

chapters.summary: Aviles describes Puerto Rico as the world's oldest colony, controlled by the U.S. government and Wall Street. She criticizes predatory debt practices, La Junta, and projects like Project Esencia that displace Puerto Ricans.
chapters.title: Aviles discusses Puerto Rico's colonial status and debt

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Today, the island is the world

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: oldest colony.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Its political and economic systems remain controlled by the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Government and its Wall Street allies.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: The resolutions we will vote on today reject the corporate takeover of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: They call for an end to the predatory debt practices that put Wall Street profits over the needs of working Puerto Ricans.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: That is a practice that is allowed by the New York State Legislature, something we can do in this state.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: They demand an end to La Junta, the unelected body that acts as a shadow government over the island.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: They reject destructive developments like Proyecto Esencia and millionaire tax havens that displace Puerto Ricans and disconnect them from their land and resources.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: A fight we are having throughout our city as we too and our communities face displacement.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: By predatory practices and the same financial institutions that are not only pillaging this city, but cities across the country.

chapters.summary: Aviles declares that New York City is home to the world's largest Puerto Rican population and stands in solidarity with the island. She concludes with 'Puerto Rico no se vende. Puerto Rico se defiende.'
chapters.title: Aviles expresses solidarity with Puerto Rico

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I'm a proud sponsor of these three resolutions, and to make it clear that New York City and state is home to the world's largest Puerto Rican population, and we unequivocally stand in solidarity

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: with our people in Puerto Rico on the island.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So hear me loud and hear me clear.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Puerto Rico no se vende.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Puerto Rico se defiende.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Puerto Rico is not for sale.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Puerto Rico will be defended.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Que viva Puerto Rico libre.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Gracias.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams invites Council Member Justin Sanchez to speak. Sanchez shares his grandfather's migration from Puerto Rico and his work as a cab driver and presser, connecting his family's story to the Puerto Rican dream.
chapters.title: Chair invites Council Member Sanchez; Sanchez shares his grandfather's story

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And let me now invite...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, so?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Or lean?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, that's me.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, hi.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, now let me invite Councilmember Sanchez to speak about his resolution.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is this on?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Buenos dias a todos.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: My name is Justin Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I have the proud honor of representing the South Bronx and one of the largest

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Puerto Rican populations and all of the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to start off by saying a little bit about my story.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: My grandfather came here from Manatee, Puerto Rico in the 60s.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I grew up in the front of multiple cabs.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: He was a yellow cab driver.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: He was a unit cab driver.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: He was a Watson cab driver.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I grew up going to the dry cleaners where he was also a presser.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And believe me, if he saw a single wrinkle on anything that I'm wearing today from wherever he is, he is coming to get me.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But that turn from when he got here to now his grandson,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Being a New York City council member is exactly why he came from Puerto Rico to New York.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It wasn't only to give himself a better opportunity, but the rest of his family.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And he had the most epic death of all time.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm not even joking.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: My grandfather died dancing salsa at the Copa.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Literally surrounded by family and friends, hitting his signature one, two, bop, heart attack right there.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's the story of us as Puerto Ricans.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Look how we laugh at something that is so sad.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But it's beautiful because it reminds us of our culture and our family and about the dreams of the people that came here before us that we have to continue fighting for.

chapters.summary: Sanchez argues that the American dream must evolve into a Puerto Rican dream. He criticizes Act 22 for promoting relocation of individual investors while denying Puerto Ricans the opportunity to build their island.
chapters.title: Sanchez discusses American dream vs. Puerto Rican dream and Act 22

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And that American dream didn't just stop when he got here.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Or when he passed, or when members of his family were able to take on big dreams.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But that American dream takes a new form in us that are the next generation.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Because we also need to build the Puerto Rican dream.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And that is a dream in which

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: unlike Act 22, to promote the relocation of individual investors,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: while also using the American government to continue to not pay taxes and deny Puerto Ricans the opportunity to continue building and creating the island and the families and the culture that we love.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But that is why I'm so proud to be here alongside my colleagues, Councilmember Aviles, and all of the people here, and everyone in this room, because together we show that it doesn't matter if you're on the island, off the island, where you come from,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But it matters that when people are coming to destroy what our families and our generations and our culture have built, we won't stand idly by because we're not only building our American dream, we're building our Puerto Rican dreams too.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams invites Council Member Yusef Salaam to offer welcoming remarks. Salaam welcomes attendees to the Schomburg Center and Harlem, noting the center's Puerto Rican roots through Arturo Schomburg.
chapters.title: Chair invites Council Member Salaam; Salaam welcomes to Harlem

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And finally, I will invite Councilmember Salam to offer some welcoming remarks to his district, of which he is justifiably very proud.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: First, may I say may the peace, mercy, and blessings from the owner of all peace, mercy, and blessings be upon each and every one of you and your families.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: You know, it's so dope to be here in the village of Harlem at the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: All of the members who are on the dais have their passports stamped forever.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Move throughout the city, of course.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: It is really a special place.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Welcome to the historic Arturo Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, and welcome to Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: It's especially meaningful to have this hearing in a place dedicated to preserving the stories, the histories, and the experiences of Black communities and the African diaspora.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The Arturo Schomburg Center

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: itself has a deep Puerto Rican roots through its namesake, Arturo Schomburg, who was born in Puerto Rico and devoted his life to documenting the history and contributions of people of African descent.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: That makes today's hearing

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: about more than just preserving the past, it's also about understanding the policies that shape the lives of our residents today.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The resolutions before us concerning Puerto Rico speak directly to the experiences of many Puerto Rican New Yorkers in our city

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: and how decisions made in Puerto Rico can have very, very real consequences for families and for communities here in New York City.

chapters.summary: Salaam provides an overview of Resolutions 28, 372, 494, and 27. He explains their focus on ending the fiscal board, repealing Act 22, stopping Project Esencia, and restricting predatory debt practices.
chapters.title: Salaam explains each Puerto Rico resolution

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Resolution 20.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: has been discussed, addresses the financial oversight and management board for Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The board was created under Promicia.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: In 2016, and under current law, its termination depends on conditions including access to credit markets and four consecutive years of balanced budgets.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: This resolution asks Congress to establish a clear date for ending that federal oversight.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Resolution 372.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Addresses tax policy in Act 22.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Its focus is on creating a more progressive tax structure and limiting revenue losses.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: For Puerto Rican New Yorkers, these questions can also become questions about housing costs, displacement, and whether economic growth creates opportunity broadly or primarily benefits those with the greatest resources.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: In Resolution 494, concerns Project Essencia in Cabo Rojo.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The proposed development is a major tourism and residential project, and there are significant disagreements about its potential economic environment, its potential

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: economic, environmental, water, housing, and community impacts.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Those questions are currently being examined in Puerto Rico, including

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: through public hearings.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And finally, Resolution 27, which strengthened New York's restrictions on the purchase of distressed sovereign debt for the purpose of litigation

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: and require good faith participation in certain debt restructurings.

chapters.summary: Salaam emphasizes that the stories of Puerto Rico and the African diaspora are connected. He thanks the committee and concludes his remarks.
chapters.title: Salaam concludes on connected stories

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: When we talk about telling our stories, we also have to recognize that our stories are connected, whether in Puerto Rico, or I'm going to say it like they say it, Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Or anywhere the Middle Passage carries the sun-kissed people.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: It's all about, it's all a part of our story.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams speaks about the importance of preserving history, especially in the current political climate. She acknowledges Assembly Member Jordan Wright and thanks colleagues who traveled to Harlem.
chapters.title: Chair Williams remarks on preserving history and acknowledges Assembly Member Wright

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: This wasn't in my remarks, but what I will say, I think no one in this room is absent of what's happening across our country.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if not now, being one of the most important moments to preserve our history,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't know what else is.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I'm just really excited to have this hearing to learn more about our research libraries and continue to do our work as a council to preserve our history.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I say our, even though we know this particular place is about a particular demographic, but it truly is our history.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge Assemblymember Jordan Wright, who's also here with us.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Can you give him a round of applause?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And now, without further ado, I want to acknowledge my colleagues who trucked all the way up to the village of Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Good morning, Council Member Sloan, my Council Member, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I'm Jordan Wright, Assembly Member, and I'm proud to represent this community in the New York State Assembly.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I want to thank Deputy Speaker Williams and the members of the committee for coming uptown and having this hearing here in Harlem at the Schomburg, where this conversation belongs.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Because when we talk about preserving black history, we're not talking about something abstract.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: We're talking about our history, Harlem's history, people who have lived here, organized here, created here, raised families here, and changed the world right from here.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: That history deserves to be protected.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Places like the Schomburg can make sure that years from now someone can pick up and actually pick up the papers, look at the photographs that made Harlem what it is today and made the world what it is today from the people who've actually lived it.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: That's what matters to me.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: And it's important that we're teaching all the things that make our culture our culture.

utterances.text: For the record, my name is Joy Bivens, but it's part of my remarks as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: My name is Joy Bivens, and I have the distinct privilege of serving as director of the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture.

chapters.summary: Bivens explains that NYPL's research centers include the Schomburg Center, the Schwarzman Building, and the Library for the Performing Arts. She emphasizes that research fuels discovery and deepens human understanding.
chapters.title: Joy Bivens discusses NYPL research centers and mission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: It's an honor to host the City Council this morning and also members of the public as my colleagues and I

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: share information about the work and offerings of the New York Public Library's research centers, including the Schomburg Center for Research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: in black culture, the Stephen A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Schwarzman Building, which focuses on humanities and social sciences, and the Library for Performing Arts, which specializes in dance, theater, music, and recorded sound.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: In our libraries, we believe that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Research fuels discovery and deepens human understanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: In an era that we know is marked by overwhelming volumes of information, fragmented and unequal access, and eroding trust, libraries stand as beacons of knowledge and access,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: They preserve the artifacts, the material culture that is critical to our collective history and critical for scholars, for writers, for educators, students, creators,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: the curious, and anyone who's hungry for intellectual exploration.

chapters.summary: Bivens describes NYPL's 55 million items, 300 databases, and partnership with RECAP. She highlights that anyone with a library card can access the collections, which are open to all New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Bivens details NYPL collections, RECAP, and accessibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So my comments go really kind of broad and then more about the Schomburg Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Our collections at the library are developed by expert curators and subject specialists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We acquire both general collections comprising currently published books, serials, databases, as well as special collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Together, NYPL's research collections total more than 55 million items, with over 70,000 books, 6,000 serials, and 1,500 linear feet of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: of special collections added annually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: These are increasingly acquired in digital formats that can be accessed remotely by students and researchers across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We also subscribe to more than 300 databases, providing online access to specialized resources in the humanities, social sciences, fine and performing arts,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Africana Studies, and Business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Our collecting scope is global, with major investments in materials from Western and Eastern Europe, Latin America, Africa, China, and India.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The library also, pardon me,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: partners with Research Collections and Preservation Consortium, pardon me, I'm gonna say that again, the Research Collections and Preservation Consortium, also known as RECAP,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: which includes Columbia, Harvard, Princeton, and Yale universities, to provide access to an additional

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: 23 million volumes of materials to our users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: What distinguishes NYPL's research offerings from those other libraries is accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We are a public research library and open access to our extraordinary collections, staff expertise,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Research services mean that anyone with a library card has access to the history we preserve, to the world of knowledge that we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: be steward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And as this committee knows, that means anyone who lives, works, or goes to school in New York State can freely engage with all of our collections and programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Now that's all of us.

chapters.summary: Bivens details the Schomburg Center's founding in 1925, its 11 million items, and its divisions: art and artifacts, Jean Blackwell Hudson Research Division, Manuscripts Archives and Rare Books, Moving Image and Recorded Sound, and Photography and Prints.
chapters.title: Bivens focuses on Schomburg Center history and collections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: About the Schomburg Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We began in 1925 as the Division of Negro Literature, History, and Prints at the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: In 1926, our collection grew exponentially with the purchase of the private library of our namesake, Arturo Alfonso Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And since its founding, the Schomburg's collections have grown to over 11 million items,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: along with hundreds of exhibitions, public programming, and a range of educational offerings we serve Harlem and the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Our collections focus on African American, African diasporic,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: and African experiences and are organized by format.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Art and artifacts includes fine and applied art and material culture objects from the 17th century to the present.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: To the present.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The Jean Blackwell Hudson Research and Reference Division holds books, serials, and microforms documenting people of African descent worldwide, with an emphasis on the Americas, the Caribbean, and Sub-Saharan Africa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Manuscripts, Archives, and Rare Books includes more than 1,000 collections of unpublished manuscripts, personal papers, rare books, including James Baldwin, Maya Angelou, Lorraine Hansberry, the list goes on and on,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: among other items that trace black diasporic life from the 16th century

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: to the present.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The moving image and recorded sound division preserves nearly 400 collections of audio and moving image materials, capturing the sounds and images of major black cultural and historical moments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And lastly, the photography and prints division houses more than one million items spanning from the 18th century to today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Providing evidence of the presence of black presence in the earliest forms of photographic technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Pardon me.

chapters.summary: Bivens highlights the Schomburg's centennial exhibition '100: A Century of Collections, Community, and Creativity' and a new exhibition on Black women artists. She also describes the Junior Scholars Program and Scholars in Residence fellowship.
chapters.title: Bivens discusses centennial, exhibitions, and programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: This year, the Schomburg Center celebrated its centennial, and one of the many ways we commemorated that milestone was with an exhibition entitled 100, A Century of Collections, Community, and Creativity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: It celebrated a century of committed collecting and dedicated stewardship by generations of Schomburg Center librarians, curators, and educators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Key elements included a 1937 signed copy of Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God, as well as sculpture and paintings by Pietro Calvi and Aaron Douglas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And then just last week, we opened a new exhibition, which you can see, called Entitled, or called Forging Ahead, Recent Acquisitions of Black Women Artists, which features the work of 21 female artists working across various

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: As part of our commitment to accessibility and engagement with the communities we serve, we host dozens of public programs and education initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And one I am most proud of is our Junior Scholars Program, a free Saturday academic program that promotes historical literacy through college-style lectures and project-based learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: It's now in its 25th year, and it has served nearly 2,500 students to date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The 2025-2026 school year engaged 140 registered...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: students in grades 6 through 12, representing all New York City boroughs, South Jersey, Connecticut, and Westchester and Rockland counties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The Schomburg Center also manages a robust event of calendars or a robust event calendar, regular public programs, book discussions, film screenings, and opportunities for our community to engage our collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We also offer competitive fellowships for academics and researchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Our Scholars in Residence program, now in its fourth decade and the first in the New York Public Library system,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: offers long and short-term fellowships to support scholars and writers working on projects that benefit from access to our collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Put it simply, the Schomburg is more than just an archive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We are a living institution that honors the past while actively engaging communities and scholars who carry that legacy forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Thank you for visiting the Schomburg today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: I really hope that you take some time to visit exhibitions, including one that looks at Arturo Schomburg's personal library, what we call the Seed Library.

chapters.summary: Bivens concludes her testimony and introduces her colleague Roberta Pineda, Executive Director of NYPL's Library for the Performing Arts.
chapters.title: Joy Bivens introduces Roberta Pineda

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Now I will turn the mic over to my colleague, Roberta Pereira.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Sorry, Roberta, I couldn't get that last name right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We're going to roll that over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We're going to roll that over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: at some point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Executive Director for NYPL's Library for the Performing Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Roberta Pineda introduces herself as the first Latina Executive Director of the Library for the Performing Arts. She describes LPA's 15 million items, hybrid research and circulating model, and collections like the Theater on Film and Tape Archive.
chapters.title: Roberta Pineda introduces herself and LPA collections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: My name is Roberta Pineda, and I am proud to be the first Latina Executive Director of the Library for the Performing Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: LPA, which is located on the Lincoln Center campus, houses one of the world's most extensive research collections with items of theater, film, dance, music, and recorded sound.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We have over 15 million items in our collection, as well as an array of circulating and reference materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Our hybrid model as both a research and circulating library was the first of its kind when we opened in 1965.

chapters.summary: Pineda highlights LPA's free public programs, including exhibitions on Martha Graham and 'Unleashed: Pets of the Performing Arts.' She notes the 60th anniversary celebration with 18 free programs and over 12,000 attendees.
chapters.title: Pineda describes LPA events and exhibitions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: On any given day, any New Yorker can walk into the library for the performing arts and find their fellow citizens engaging with everything,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: including an 80s era Shakespeare performance or an exhibition showcasing the work of a Broadway costume designer, a film screening, or simply browsing an archive like Gregory Hines'collection of American tap dance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Our theater on film and tape archive includes over 6,000 live theater performances from 1970 onward and has served for decades as a free,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: of a kind resource for theater professionals, scholars, students, and other interested parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We also hold the world's largest collection of theater photographs, over 2,000 wax cylinder recordings, 2,875 original live dance performances, over 1,000 items in the Martha Graham archive,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: 300 boxes in the Meredith Monk archive, and collections from Hal Prince, Lou Reed, and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: LPA also manages an ongoing calendar of noteworthy events and exhibitions showcasing the work of artists whose contributions have shaped or pushed the boundaries of society and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Our calendar currently includes staff-led tours of our recent exhibition,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Martha Graham, the Mother of Psychological Dance, which highlights the legacy of Graham and her dance technique, as well as the company, which is the oldest continuously operating dance company in the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Theater Play Club, a book club for plays, where this month they will be discussing the play Anna in the Tropics by Nilo Cruz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: An all-ages back-to-school free screening of E.T.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: In our new classic series, next Saturday if anybody wants to come at 1 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And our newest offering, Unleashed, Pets of the Performing Arts, an exhibition exploring the unique bonds between iconic art

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: artists and their animal companions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: All of these are free, all of these are available for anybody just walked in through our doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We recently celebrated our 60th anniversary with 18 free public programs over the course of one week across venues at the library, Lincoln Center, and online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: The events included classes for all ages, staged musical theater readings, and even dance parties, and we exceeded an attendance of over 12,000 people.

chapters.summary: Pineda describes LPA's Dance Research Fellowship and Across the Crowded Room Fellowship. She emphasizes that all materials are accessible to anyone with a free library card and that the library provides welcoming spaces for all New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Pineda discusses fellowships and accessibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: LPA supports academics and performance alike through fellowship opportunities, like our Dance Research Fellowship, which provides a stipend and dedicated librarian support to dance scholars and performers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: seeking to advance their work with topics including dance and democracy, dance and ecology, and the 75th anniversary of the Jerome Robbins Dance Division.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: The Across the Crowded Room Fellowship invites new musical theater writers, performers, and directors to come to the library, meet each other, and create a 20-minute musical, often based on library special collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Participants receive feedback from industry leaders, and six fellowships have been awarded over the past three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Perhaps more important than what we offer is how accessible these offerings are to everyday New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: All of these materials and features are part of NYPL's holdings, meaning they are not limited to students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: and researchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: The only requirement is a library card, which is completely free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: An important part of access is making all New Yorkers feel welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: That is why we also provide quiet study areas, desks, power outlets, and computers throughout the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Whether sifting through an archive for inspiration, admiring the work of current artists, or simply securing a quiet desk with a power outlet,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: the Library for the Performing Arts is where world-class performing arts scholarship and everyday New York life come together on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Pineda introduces her colleague Julie Golia, Director of the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Library at the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building.
chapters.title: Roberta Pineda introduces Julie Golia

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Please welcome my colleague, Julie Golia, Director of the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Library at the Stephen A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Schwarzman Building.

chapters.summary: Julie Golia thanks the committee and introduces the Schwarzman Building as NYPL's most recognized location. She notes it welcomes 3.8 million visitors a year and supports researchers across 11 reading rooms.
chapters.title: Julie Golia introduces Schwarzman Building

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Thank you, Roberta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And thank you to the chair, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of this committee for the opportunity for all of us to share our work today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The Stephen A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Schwarzman Building is the New York Public Library's most recognized location, renowned for its extraordinary collections and its commitment to providing free and equal access to its resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: This will not be the first or last time you'll hear me say, all you need is a library card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Welcoming 3.8 million visitors a year, we support researchers of all levels and backgrounds across 11

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: reading rooms, and we introduce visitors to the wonders of libraries through exhibitions, programs, tours, and educational outreach.

chapters.summary: Golia details the Schwarzman Building's collections, including 350,000 rare books, nearly half a million maps, and the Polonsky Exhibition of Treasures. She highlights exhibitions like 'Declaring America' and 'Wepa' on Puerto Rican comics.
chapters.title: Golia describes Schwarzman collections and exhibitions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our mission is to support and generate research scholarship and thought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: As with LPA and Schomburg, the only requirement to engage with our tens of millions of materials is a library card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our collections span formats, books, archives, maps, photos, print, art, magazines and newspapers, recorded sound, video, and we even preserve digital materials like emails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our world-class archival collections draw researchers studying the American Revolution, the Civil War, New York City social history, the history of publishing and journalism, and L.A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: LGBTQ plus history, among many other areas of study.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The collection includes 350,000 rare books with historical volumes like the first Gutenberg Bible to reach the Americas, alongside nearly half a million maps and atlases spanning the 16th to the 21st centuries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We house one of the country's great print and photography collections and an expansive periodicals collection where recently arrived New Yorkers can find daily issues of dozens of foreign newspapers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: While the New York Public Library's primary audience is New Yorkers, the Schwarzman Building also doubles as one of New York City's top tourist attractions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Through our exhibitions and displays, we seek to immerse visitors from around the country and the world in the wonders of libraries and give them the opportunity to see our collections come to life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our beloved permanent exhibition, the Polonsky Exhibition of the New York Public Library's Treasures, features a rotating showcase of some of the most extraordinary items from our holdings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The items in this exhibition tell the stories of people, places, and moments spanning 4,000 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: From the emergence of the written word to the present day, visitors will encounter manuscripts,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: artworks, letters, still and moving images, and recordings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Everything from the original Winnie the Pooh dolls to Malcolm X's briefcase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: To commemorate America's 250th birthday this year, the Schwarzman Building opened Declaring America, 1776 and Beyond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: A three-gallery exhibition which unpacks the complex, diverse, and powerful stories of the American Revolution from 1776 to today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We recently concluded New York, an exhibition which explored often overlooked histories of Middle Eastern and North African immigration to New York City from the late 19th century to the present.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And we recently closed Weipa, an exhibition that highlighted the breathtaking contributions of Puerto Ricans to the world of comics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Wepa.

chapters.summary: Golia describes the 'Live from NYPL' series and 'Library After Hours' events. She also highlights the Vartan Gregorian Center for Research in the Humanities, which offers scholar residencies and fellowships.
chapters.title: Golia discusses programming and research center

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The Schwarzman Building oversees robust engagement with the public and researchers alike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Live from NYPL is the library's premier public programming series, bringing prominent writers, artists, intellectuals, and public figures to the library for discussions and stage appearances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Past programs have featured Lina Khan and Jay-Z.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And our current fall calendar includes Hilton Alls, George Saunders, and Jill Lepore, among others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our Library After Hours series connects patrons to research libraries'collections through

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: through themed, curated building takeovers, often billed as the library's most cerebral happy hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Topics range from children's literature to Pride Month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The Shoresman Building also offers extensive resources and opportunities for researchers and scholars through our Vartan Gregorian Center for Research in the Humanities, which serves as a hub for an array of research resources and services aimed at

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: fostering scholarly practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Specific offerings include a scholar residency program with up to 350 scholars working across five study rooms with tailored collection access,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: eight short to long-term research fellowships and public classes, and primary source educational experiences designed to turn scholars and beginners into researchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: From the Gutenberg Bible to Declaring America to a fellowship recipient deep in research to a young New Yorker standing in line for the city's most cerebral happy hour,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: the Shoresman Building is where extraordinary scholarship and open public access are one and the same.

chapters.summary: Golia reports that NYPL research libraries circulated 444,000 items and received 4.3 million visitors in FY26. She notes that 63% of the research libraries' budget comes from private funding, 29% from the city, and 8% from the state.
chapters.title: Golia discusses usage data and funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Now I'm going to shift to talking more broadly about our research library's impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Together, these three research libraries'commitment to accessibility is supported by our usage data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: In the fiscal year 26, we circulated 444,000 research items.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: During

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: During this same period, our research libraries received over 4.3 million visitors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Stewarding collections of this scale and keeping them free and open to all requires significant and sustained investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: NYPL's research libraries are primarily supported by private fundings at 63% of their total budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The remaining 37% of the budget comes from public funds, with 29% from the city and 8% from the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The Schomburg Junior Scholars Program, which Joy talked about, is nearly 70% supported by city funds, with $165,000

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: allocated by the city council in the FY27 adopted budget, and we thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We are deeply appreciative of the city's support of the research libraries, and we look forward to working with the administration and the council for continued support.

chapters.summary: Golia emphasizes that NYPL's research centers are freely accessible to all New Yorkers. She outlines future plans to expand digital access, improve research experience, and increase preservation efforts, calling for increased investment.
chapters.title: Golia concludes on accessibility and future plans

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We are proud that our research centers cover such a wide range of cultural, community, academic, and artistic aspects of the human experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And while the breadth and depth of our offerings are what often garners attention, what we are most proud of is the fact that they are all freely accessible to New Yorkers of all walks of life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: All of this is only possible because of our expert staff, librarians, technical assistants, curators, and pages who maintain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: both the quality and variety of our collections, as well as their accessibility to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: In the next five years, we plan to take this commitment even further by extending digital access to our collections, improving the research experience of in-person and online users, doubling down on our preservation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: efforts, expanding fellowship opportunities, and reaching the broader public with compelling exhibitions and programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The realization of these ambitious goals will not be possible without increased investment in libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We look forward to your continued support to ensure our research libraries remain among the most vital public goods that the city provides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: With my colleagues, we thank you for the opportunity to testify and are happy to answer any questions you might have.

chapters.summary: Shakira Smalls introduces herself as Executive Director of Queens Public Library's Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center. She describes QPL's 50 digital research databases and specialized print collections.
chapters.title: Shakira Smalls introduces herself and QPL services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: My name is Shakira Smalls, and I'm the Executive Director for Queens Public Library's Langston Hughes Community Library and Culture Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: On behalf of our President and CEO, Dennis Walcott, thank you, Deputy Speaker and Chair Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Williams, and the members of this committee for the opportunity to speak about the library's research collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I also want to thank New York Public Libraries for hosting today's event.

chapters.summary: Smalls details the Langston Hughes Community Library's founding in 1969 and its Black Heritage Reference Center. She highlights collections including the Langston Hughes Collection, Art Collection, and Adele Cohen Music Collection.
chapters.title: Smalls describes Langston Hughes collections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It is Queens Public Library's highest responsibility to encourage and support exploration and learning, enabling people to grow and gain a deeper understanding of the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In this effort, all QPL services, including our vast collection, are free, open to the public, and accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We offer more than 50 digital research databases, including the New York Times Digital Collection, Fiero Learning, LinkedIn Learning, and America's Voice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In addition, we offer specialized print collections, which reside at the library branch I oversee, as well as our central library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Langston Hughes Community Library and Culture Center was established in 1969 through a grassroots movement and it's home to the Black Heritage Reference Center for Queens County.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The center stands as a testament to the richness and depth of Black history

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: with its extraordinary collections representing diverse subjects, including African history, the African diaspora, slavery, civil rights movements, critical race theory, racism, African American art, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We have encyclopedias, primary source documents, and writings by prominent figures such as Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, and Barack Obama.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: At the Langston Hughes Library, we are fortunate to have collections that showcase the everlasting impact the legendary Harlem Renaissance writer and activist had on society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: These include the Langston Hughes Collection, a public circulating collection featuring materials written by and about the prolific writer and poet Laurette.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Langston Hughes Art Collection, a non-circulating collection comprised of prints, posters, paintings, African textiles, kente cloths, and African sculptures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And the Adele Cohen Music Collection, which contains lyrics, librettos, and other original works by Langston Hughes set to music.

chapters.summary: Smalls describes the Black Heritage Video Collection, Amistad Research Center Microfilm Collection, and Black Newspaper Microfilm Collection. She also discusses the weekly Sankofa series that explores Black culture topics.
chapters.title: Smalls details Black Heritage collections and Sankofa series

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In addition, we have collections that advance the education and preservation of Black culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Black Heritage Video Collection focuses specifically on the Black experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Amistad Research Center Microfilm Collection includes the papers of many American luminaries, such as County Cullen, Fannie Lou Hamer, Freddie Washington, and Mary McLeod Bethune.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Black Newspaper Microfilm Collection contains newspaper titles dating back to the 1800s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: To complement the collection, we offer our weekly Sankofa series where customers can explore rotating topics related to black culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: For the month of August, we hosted four programs on black fashion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In this current month, we have been discussing 60 years of the Black Panthers history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The series gives customers who may otherwise not engage with the Black Heritage Research Center as scholars or researchers the opportunity to explore this living collection's many historical works and cultural resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Additionally, with support from the City Council Coalition for Theaters of Color Initiative, we offer dance, music, and storytelling performances that celebrate and spotlight the subjects covered in our specialized collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Approximately half of the Black Heritage Collection is publicly circulated, making it one of the largest public circulating collections on a Black experience in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Having a large repository devoted to Black-authored or Black-centric works that can be requested and borrowed by anyone ensures all communities can learn and benefit from these resources.

chapters.summary: Smalls outlines QPL's Central Library archives, including 36,000 books, 4,500 maps, and 105,000 photographs. She also describes the Carter G. Woodson Reference Collection, Augusta Baker Collection, and International Language Collection.
chapters.title: Smalls describes Central Library archives and other collections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Queens Public Library's Central Library supports our 66 locations across the borough and serves as a destination for research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Open seven days a week, the archives at QPL contain primary and secondary resources documenting local history available to anyone who visits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In addition, our staff is regularly digitizing and cataloging the archives content, which includes approximately 36,000

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: 1,000 books and volumes of serials, 4,500 maps, and 105,000 photographs and other documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Carter G.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Woodson Reference Collection is comprised of more than 4,000 reference materials covering various aspects of African American culture and life with a focus on slavery,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: contemporary African American life, slave narratives, and the papers of the nation's most influential black leaders, including Frederick Douglass and Booker T.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Washington.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Located in our Children's Library Discovery Center, the Augusta Baker Collection examines the history of the African American experience through the lens of children's literature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: A pioneering children's librarian, master storyteller, and native of St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Albans, Queens, Augusta Baker built the collection throughout her life, which culminated in 500 titles spanning from the 1940s to the late 20th century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It also features books about Negro life for children, a resource guide Baker published in 1963 to assist librarians and library users in finding reading materials that depict black without bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Additionally, at Central Library, individuals can study the Belcher Hyde and Sanborn Company maps that detail the building structures in Queens and Greater Long Island,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: including their size, address, building materials, and other information dating back to 1898.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The Long Island Daily Press photographed more collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: a newspaper that was established in 1821 and published in the Jamaica neighborhood until 1977.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
