utterances.text: The International Language Collection, an essential asset for the library system serving the world's borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It has fiction and nonfiction materials in 35 languages, including Bengali, Japanese, Polish, Spanish, and Urdu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It also includes the Graceman Memorial Collection, which contains more than 1,350 reference books honoring the Chinese language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And QPL's Music Score Collection, which is publicly circulated and has more than 44,000 volumes of sheet music, lyrics, teaching resources, and more, spanning different genres, languages, and instruments.

chapters.summary: Smalls explains how QPL's research collections provide context for contemporary events like flooding in Southeast Queens. She thanks the City Council for its support and emphasizes the importance of diverse collections.
chapters.title: Smalls discusses research collections' role and thanks council

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Our research collections are crucial in providing insight and context to contemporary events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: With the rise of extreme weather, the archives at QPL research and compile the history of flooding in Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It chronicles how an area of mostly marshland became a farming community, the population boom that led to inadequate infrastructure for the area, and ongoing improvement efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Their investigation reveals that flooding in Southeast Queens is a longstanding challenge that has been exasperated by climate change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Through the preservation and development of our collections, these historical and contemporary resources shield against misinformation and distortion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: The library plays a crucial role in helping the public properly navigate and analyze data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Not only do our talented staff answer questions and lend guidance, but QPL also offers classes on improving necessary research skills, deciphering information, and using our databases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Queens Public Library's collection, whether our special collection at the Black Heritage Reference Center or at Central Library or any of our branch collection across the borough, allow individuals to immerse themselves in the past and present,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: broadening and deepening their perspectives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: At a time when libraries are being attacked for giving people the right to seek and access diverse points of view,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: we must continue to stand against bigotry, challenge historical misconceptions, foster critical thinking, encourage empathy, and inspire curiosity by ensuring our collections are diverse,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: well-maintained, and readily available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We are grateful to our elected officials, especially the New York City Council, for championing the city's public library systems and the work we do on a daily basis, and we hope to count on your support in the years ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Again, Deputy Chair, thank you so much for allowing us to testify today.

chapters.summary: Natiba Guy-Clement introduces herself as Director of Special Collections at the Center for Brooklyn History. She shares that she started her career at the Schomburg Center as a library page over 25 years ago.
chapters.title: Natiba Guy-Clement introduces herself and connection to Schomburg

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: My name is Nativa Guy-Clement, and I am the Director of Special Collections at the Center for Brooklyn History at Brooklyn Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Thank you to members of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations, and the entire City Council,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: for providing us with an opportunity today to celebrate, highlight, and advocate for the work that we do in preserving New York City's history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I'd like to start today by saying how grateful I am to be here today to speak on behalf of the research collections and the work we do at the Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And to be doing that at a place that I started my career in research libraries over 25 years ago as a library page.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I was also a new immigrant to the U.S., a new Harlem resident, and a new student at Hunter College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: The introduction I received to research collections here at the Schomburg Center so many years ago has been carried with me throughout my career, which is a testament to the power and impact of research libraries and the collections that they steward.

chapters.summary: Guy-Clement explains that the Center for Brooklyn History was formed in 2020 by merging Brooklyn Public Library and the Brooklyn Historical Society. It holds tens of thousands of books, 1,600 archival collections, and hundreds of thousands of photographs.
chapters.title: Guy-Clement describes Center for Brooklyn History formation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Brooklyn is not just a place with a remarkable history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It is a place whose history has shaped New York City and the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: The Center for Brooklyn History exists to make sure that history is collected, preserved, studied, and accessible to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: In 2020, Brooklyn Public Library and the then Brooklyn Historical Society joined together,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: bringing the borough's two most significant historical collections about Brooklyn under one roof and creating the Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: The partnership paired the Historical Society's deep archival holdings with BPL's Brooklyn collection and the reach of a 62-location public library system, with the goal of making Brooklyn's history more accessible to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Today, the Center for Brooklyn History holds tens of thousands of books, more than 1,600 archival collections, hundreds of thousands of photographs, maps, artifacts, paintings, newspapers, and oral history interviews.

chapters.summary: Guy-Clement describes collections including Revolutionary War artifacts, Brooklyn CORE civil rights materials, and the Greenpoint Environmental History Project. She also discusses digital collections and community-donated yearbooks.
chapters.title: Guy-Clement details collections and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Our collections reflect Brooklyn's past and present in many ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: They include items such as artifacts from the Revolutionary War that highlight the fraught and harrowing fight for America's freedom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Documents related to the emancipation of enslaved people in America and the actions that led to the Civil War.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It reflects Brooklyn's fight for civil rights in collections like Brooklyn Core,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: which looks at activism in Brooklyn and includes images of sit-ins, boycotts, as well as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: an interesting notebook that documented protester arrests and how the organization assisted those arrested with legal support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It also covers more contemporary issues as well, such as gentrification and changing communities, and collections like the Greenpoint Environmental History Project that documents years of pollution and community action towards cleaner air and water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: In addition to our physical collections, we are continuously building on our digital collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: That ranges from born digital to digitized materials, and our web archive that allows us to save Brooklyn websites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: My personal favorite collections are ones that document the lives of regular Brooklynites, like our Brooklyn Schools collection, which holds hundreds of yearbooks, school newspapers, and other memorabilia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And a recently processed collection, the Butcher and Johnson family papers about a Brooklyn family and the Great Migration,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: as they wove their lives through Barbados, Panama, Cuba, and New Orleans to finally settle down in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Collections like these allow us to signal to everyone that their stories belong in the archives.

chapters.summary: Guy-Clement explains that CBH provides access through the Othmer Library, public programs, and off-site exhibitions. She notes that CBH lacks dedicated city operating funding and has absorbed $2.6 million in operating costs.
chapters.title: Guy-Clement discusses access, exhibitions, and funding needs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And speaking of belonging in the archives, we are about to launch a call for community donated yearbooks to add to our collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So if any of the esteemed Brooklyn members of the committee are interested in donating theirs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Please let me know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Our collections are exceptionally rich, but we also know they do not yet represent every Brooklyn community equally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Collecting today's Brooklyn and filling silences in the historical record is part of the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Access to these collections take many forms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Researchers can work directly with our original materials in the Othmer Library,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: but the Center for Brooklyn History also brings Brooklyn history to people through public programs, education initiatives, exhibitions, and digital resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Increasingly, that work happens across Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Through cross-borough genealogy workshops focused on using our digital collections, branch-based projects, and off-site exhibitions such as Memories Matter at the Euclid Avenue subway station.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We are bringing materials and stories from the collection into neighborhoods across the borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We're also excited to continue to share our collections through storytelling, and we are currently in the midst of planning two new exhibitions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: one which commemorates the 200th anniversary of the abolition of slavery in New York State, and another, Mapping Puerto Rican Brooklyn, which looks at the lives and the history of Puerto Ricans in the borough.

chapters.summary: Guy-Clement calls for sustained public investment to help CBH collect a more representative record of Brooklyn. She thanks the committee and her fellow panelists.
chapters.title: Guy-Clement concludes on need for funding and thanks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We are doing this work without any dedicated city operating funding for Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Despite repetitive requests for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: direct support, Brooklyn Public Library has absorbed 2.6 million in operating costs through our existing city funding, further stretching resources already supporting 62 locations across Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: With sustained public investment, Center for Brooklyn History can collect a record that more fully represents Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Preserve it for future generations, and ensure that a student or researcher or any curious resident can encounter that history, whether they come to CBH, visit their neighborhood library, or find us online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Brooklyn history did not end in 1898 when it became part of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: With your support, we hope to continue telling the story of Brooklyn's history to future generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, as well as thank you to my fellow panelists and just hearing about the work that they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Thank you guys as well.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks how many people use the research collections each year and whether they have disaggregated data. Julie Golia, Natiba Guy-Clement, and Shakira Smalls provide usage statistics and discuss challenges in categorizing researchers versus general visitors.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about usage data; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, I just want to acknowledge that we have been joined by Councilmember Stevens and Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't think we covered this, maybe we did in some of the testimonies, but if you could just share how many people use the research collections each year,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and if you have any disaggregated data around residents, students, independent researchers, genealogists, journalists, artists, or academic scholars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I can speak for the New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We think about visitors as well as users, and so our visitorship is incredibly high across the three research centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We received 4.3 million visitors in the last fiscal year, which is a remarkable number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: A small fraction of those are users, and one way that we think about our usership, which can be more challenging to kind of disambiguate, is through our collection use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We circulated about 440,000 items in the past year across our three research libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And one of the challenges that we have around giving a hard and fast number around what a researcher is, is that we try to be very, very broad in how we define this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so, for example, at my building at 42nd Street, many of our users don't actually access the collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We just launched this sort of amazing community board in the Rosemaine Reading Room where we ask people what they're doing there today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And some of our sort of most popular answers are, I'm working on my chemistry homework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: That chemistry, that student does not necessarily have to have a library card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so we are always thinking about really creative ways of trying to be able to measure and disambiguate our visitorship, our more tourist-focused visitorship from our usership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: But we also take every opportunity to...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: turn a visitor or a tourist into a researcher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And I can speak for a Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It's kind of along the lines of what Julie is saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So for CBH, we had about 50,000 visitors in FY 2026, with nearly 10,000 using the library for research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Well, I should say visiting the library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We tend to not break our visitors down by what they're doing, but we do look at who are accessing our material versus people who are just visiting the space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: A big part of it is that we want our patrons, we want to serve them equally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We want people who come to our space to eventually feel comfortable using us for research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we really do love just being open space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And it's kind of in line with our ethos for libraries, where we believe that all of our spaces are for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And this approach kind of just gives people a better sense of comfort in spaces that may feel intimidating otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And in alignment with my colleagues, QPL, the customer visit, cannot comprehensively be tracked, but we do know that about 50% of the people who do utilize our QPL archive

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: tend to be researchers, while another 50% tend to be for personal reasoning.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams jokes about walking and chewing gum, then transitions to the Puerto Rico resolutions. She introduces Senator Adrian Gonzalez Costa, who is joining from Puerto Rico on Zoom.
chapters.title: Chair Williams transitions to Puerto Rico testimony; introduces Senator Gonzalez Costa

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How many people can walk and chew gum at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Nobody?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, well, life will force you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And with that said, we're going to just walk.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and chew gum at the same time, because while this hearing is an oversight hearing about our research collections, we are also hearing some very important resolutions, and we do have a senator from

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Puerto Rico on the Zoom, and as many elected officials know, I'm sure his schedule is extremely busy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we are gonna go to Senator Adrian Gonzalez Costa, who is joining us from Puerto Rico on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, and thank you for the privilege of addressing to you and as a, you know, as a senator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair and members of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: My name is Adrian Gonzalez Costa, and I have the honor of appearing before you as a senator of the Puerto Rican Independence Party, representing the people of Puerto Rico as a senator at large.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: I come before you today to express my strong support for the resolutions addressing Project Essencia, the Financial Oversight and Management Board, and the repeal of Act 22 of 2012.

chapters.summary: Senator Gonzalez Costa explains that Project Esencia raises concerns about privatization of coastline, protection of natural resources, and displacement of Puerto Rican communities. He argues development cannot come at the expense of beaches, ecosystems, and archaeological heritage.
chapters.title: Senator Gonzalez Costa discusses Project Esencia

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: These are not isolated issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: They are part of a larger struggle over Puerto Rico's land, resources, democracy, and economic future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: The development of Project Exencia has generated concerns regarding the privatization and commercialization of our coastline, the protection of our natural resources, especially water, and the displacement of Puerto Rican communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Development cannot come at the expense of our beaches, ecosystems, our archaeology,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: archaeological heritage, or the right of our people to remain on their own land.

chapters.summary: Senator Gonzalez Costa criticizes the Fiscal Oversight and Management Board (La Junta) as an unelected body with extraordinary powers. He argues Puerto Rico's future must be decided democratically by Puerto Ricans themselves.
chapters.title: Senator Gonzalez Costa discusses La Junta

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: On the other hand, the Fiscal Oversight and Management Board, La Junta, represents another fundamental problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Decisions affecting the lives of millions of Puerto Ricans have been placed in the hands of an unelected body with extraordinary powers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: From our perspective as an independence movement, Puerto Rico's future must be decided democratically by Puerto Ricans themselves, not by a board named single-handedly by the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Government.

chapters.summary: Senator Gonzalez Costa says Act 22 provides extraordinary tax advantages to wealthy individuals while ordinary Puerto Ricans face displacement and economic insecurity. He opposes an economic model where benefits are privatized and costs are socialized.
chapters.title: Senator Gonzalez Costa discusses Act 22

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Lastly, Act 22 and its equivalents has contributed to an economic model that provides extraordinary tax advantages to wealthy individuals,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: while ordinary Puerto Ricans continue to face displacement, rising housing costs, and economic insecurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: We are not opposed to development or investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: We are opposed to an economic model in which the benefits are privatized while the costs are socialized and borne by the Puerto Rican people.

chapters.summary: Senator Gonzalez Costa highlights the deep historic relationship between New York and Puerto Rico. He concludes that Puerto Rico is not a commodity, its land is not a tax shelter, and its democracy should not be governed by an unelected board.
chapters.title: Senator Gonzalez Costa concludes on NY-PR relationship

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: New York has a deep and historic relationship with Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Millions of Puerto Ricans live in this city and have contributed enormously to its culture, economy, and civic life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: That is why we support resolutions that are discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Puerto Rico is not a commodity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Our land is not a tax shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: and our democracy should not be governed by an unelected board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: The people of Puerto Rico deserve their right to determine their own future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Adrián González Costa
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and have a nice day.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks whether the public is sufficiently aware of the research collections and how word should be spread. Roberta Pineda, Shakira Smalls, and Natiba Guy-Clement describe outreach efforts, social media, school partnerships, and capacity challenges.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about public awareness; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Senator, and I don't know if you can hear, but people are clapping.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, back to the libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much for practicing walking and chewing gum at the same time today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We have heard this morning about the substantial research and reference centers and collections housed in our library systems.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you believe that the public is sufficiently aware of them and the work they do?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If not, how should the word be spread?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I know while I might be familiar with some of the research libraries, I stopped by the performance library before I've been to the Langston Hughes Center in Corona.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't know how many people actually know if you're not like wonky and nerdy and, you know, because this is super cool, but I'm like, this just might be my nerdy brain, not my like average New Yorker brain, like just living life.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So how do people learn about your centers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: I can respond on behalf of NYPL and specifically the Library for the Performing Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So to answer your first question, no, not enough people know about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And having the opportunity to be here to talk about it, I think it's an incredible first step.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And I think that we think about all of this work that we can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: I think my colleagues and I have been talking a lot about how can we talk about this work online, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So to give an example, the Library for the Performing Arts, last summer, we actually had an opportunity to do a panel celebrating the 50th anniversary of a chorus line on Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And then we actually did a special pop-up performance outside the library where we had cast members from 50 years of a chorus line join in an impromptu performance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And we're able to share that online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And we had millions of views, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And so from all of those views, we have more people coming in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: At the Library for the Performing Arts, just in the past year, we've actually have increased our...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: people visiting by 58%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: One of the ways we did that is by making the space more welcoming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: It was also by reaching out to the schools nearby.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We're right across the street from LaGuardia, from MLK, and all the schools there, and talking to those students and inviting them in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So I think that there's a lot more work that we can do, but it's all potential because these collections are incredible and more people should know about them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I will piggyback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: No, a lot of people do not know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I'm sure that as each one of us gave our testimony that we were learning more and more about each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So we're not even working together in our full capacity, but we will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: In addition to that, again, being here, being able to amplify our voices, being able to amplify the collection is also part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We have countless newsletters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We have social media accounts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We have outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We go inside of all of these facilities that are interested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: But if you don't know, you're not going to meet us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: If you're not signed up to our social media or following us, you still won't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So the reality is, you know, for me, capacity is a huge thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Do we have enough people that can go outside of our library to be able to amplify the services that we offer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Do we, are we able to make sure that every single person in New York City, not just Queens, but everyone can actually, you know, follow us on social media?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: But it's not there, so there's so many things that we can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: It's great opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: But thank you for sharing your elected officials because my Chanel Thomas Henry, she just volunteered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: to perform based off of you sharing your program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: But these are always, there's always forums.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I believe the last time I saw Joy was at this forum a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So these forums started, and then we just have to continue it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And you guys can also continue to do what you do by amplifying us and feeling free to put us in contact with those that need to be in contact with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker, I feel like that question was specifically for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I think for us at CBH, we have the added challenge of kind of being new.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We changed, we were another institution, we changed names, so also getting that name recognition for us, it's a very big deal and it's something that we are trying to do every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do a lot, of course, social media, follow us at Brooklyn History if you are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We try to reach people that way because we know that people are chronically online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: But in terms of our building, we do a lot of work with students as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a program called Brooklyn Connections where we teach students as early as fourth grade how to do archival research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And we work with hundreds of schools in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we really believe in getting kids in our building and getting them in young so that they understand what a research library is and what archives are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we always feel like that's a good way to kind of start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Of course, forums like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We also do a lot of community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have an exhibition that's in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we really are trying to get ourselves out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do a lot of tabling at community events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Over the summer, I was at the Laundromat Project's 20th anniversary field day, which was a lot of fun.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We were able to bring some of our collections out to the community so that they could see what we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So just many ways, but of course, having more people know about us and talk about us, it's really, really a big help.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks what significant parts of New York City's history are inadequately represented in the libraries' holdings. Joy Bivens, Natiba Guy-Clement, Shakira Smalls, and Julie Golia discuss gaps in women, LGBTQ, indigenous, disabled, and other communities.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about underrepresented histories; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, what significant parts of New York City's history do you believe are inadequately represented in your holdings today?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Although I feel like it was very diverse, and I love the Puerto Rican innuendos and all the different libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I was like, that's so cool and so relevant today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So if you could just share if there are any communities, neighborhoods, languages, industries, movements, or periods that you might be actively trying to document.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know Brooklyn Public Library talked a lot about like archiving the now, but just wanted to know if there's any other folks and histories that you feel are not represented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of how to best answer the question because I feel like it could go a few different ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: I think that despite being more than half of the population, women are always underrepresented in our collection holdings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And for the last five years here at the Schomburg, we've been actively pursuing female creators and trying to address that gap within the collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Once you start to address one gap, then you notice where the other gaps are, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Because if we are to really kind of fully address

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: For the Schomburg African diasporic history, you start to notice where and what is missing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So for the last few years, we've really been looking at how are we collecting women, women's work, women's artwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And that is, you know, fortunately, we have an opportunity to represent that in an exhibition that we just opened, the Forging Ahead exhibition that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: But I think

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: There are a lot of different communities that are not necessarily represented in any of our holdings, and we have our spidey senses up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And then that creates new work to do, new communities to pursue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And I think each of us could probably speak to probably two or three that we would really like to pursue into the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So we've started that here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: That will kind of spawn different new collecting into the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Once new curators and new subject specialists are coming into our fray, they will bring different eyes to this work as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So yes, we all have gaps in our collections, in our holdings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Yeah, one of the things that we actually wrote into our policy that we use to develop our collection are our known gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we're pretty knowledgeable of what those are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So LGBTQ communities, indigenous communities, neighborhoods in Brooklyn, Flatbush, Sunset Park, Latinx communities, Asian communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we're very aware of what they are and we're actively working towards filling those gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: A lot of the work that we want to do, you know, you want to collect about these neighborhoods and these people, but you also want to be doing it in a way that it is collaborative with those communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So that's something that's also really important for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We don't want to just go and be like, here, give us your stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We want to be working with our community members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So that's really, really important for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Biggest ways that we find out what people are asking for is our reference team, our team of archivists and librarians who are constantly meeting with the public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: and can answer these questions, check to see what we have in our collections that can answer those questions, and we can flag it when we don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So that's how we approach that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And what Joyce said, every time you open up something new, it's just more and more stories that you're missing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: But if I had to choose one for today's conversation, I'm going to say the disabled population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I feel for me specifically that, you know, we tend to do better when things are in our face and it's very easy for things to be forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And I have an amazing employee and she's 100% deaf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So working with that and being able to accommodate her and she's introducing us to her culture to be able to explain to us, I can do everything you can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And sometimes we overlook that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So I would really love to delve deeper into a disabled collection and being able to make sure their voices are amplified as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I wanted to say one more thing about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And we all have the privilege of being part of research collections that are also associated with branches that represent all the diversity of the neighborhoods of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our collections should always strive to be as diverse as our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so we have this opportunity, per what Ntiba said, to partner with colleagues and neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Not to say, oh, let us take your stuff, but to say, how can we support your own preservation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: How can you weigh in on the ongoing preservation of your collections?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And I think that is the special sauce of being a research library associated with a branch system, is that we get to serve our communities on the everyday and then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: work to preserve their history until the world stops moving.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks whether the city budget provides sufficient support for research centers and what percentage of each library system's city budget goes to research collections. Joy Bivens, Shakira Smalls, and Natiba Guy-Clement provide funding details and needs.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about city budget support; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I love that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just one more question, because I know my colleagues have questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know people want to testify, so I don't want to take up too much time.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But Nativa did touch on it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's always important to ask these questions, even outside of our budget cycle.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But does the city budget provide sufficient support for these centers and collections?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If not, what additional funding is needed from the city?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then if you could just share what percentage of the city budget allocated to each library system goes to support its research centers and collections.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if you have the amount, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So Julie mentioned this during her testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: 37% of our budget comes from public funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: 29% of that is city funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: 8% of that is state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So the answer to do we need more money is always yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: It's yes, yes, yes, and yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And I think that what that provides is an opportunity for us to make sure that our capacity is appropriate to serve our communities and to preserve these materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: I think I speak for everybody, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So 95% of Queens Public Library's funding relies on city funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: However, we do not get any funding from the city for our research collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We are fortunate to get the Coalition for Theaters of Color that amplifies our research collection, but we do not have any city funding specifically for our research collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Yes, and as I said in our testimony, we just rely on the general city funding for all of Brooklyn Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We also get about 20% in private funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We've been fortunate to also have received discretionary grants from a few of our council members and from the New York State Assembly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: If we had more funding, of course, we would want to just do more, have more kids in our building, have more exhibitions, be able to better preserve our collections,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: looking to ways to store our collections so that it doesn't impact researcher use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we have a wish list on our end if we did have more funding.

chapters.summary: Council Member Crystal Hudson asks what percentage of research collections are fully cataloged and digitized, and how they decide what gets digitized first. Julie Golia, Roberta Pineda, Shakira Smalls, and Natiba Guy-Clement explain their processes and challenges.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson asks about cataloging and digitization; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And with that, I'll turn it to Councilmember Hudson for questions, followed by Councilmember Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I do think I've found recently, sorry, I'm over here, not recently, in the last few years, one of my mother's old yearbooks.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I will definitely follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: On that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask just a question with regards to the percentage of your research collections that are fully cataloged or processed and discoverable to the public.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What percentage of significant collections has been digitized and how do you decide what gets digitized first?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We have about 55 million items, and they are housed across dozens of different divisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: So I want to make sure we get you the right numbers on the cataloging question, but it is an incredibly complex question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: In many cases, very significant portions of our collection are cataloged and accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: In other places, especially with particular kinds of formats and special collections, we have more challenges around this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: To the point you asked, the question you asked earlier about things that we would use funding for, it is very difficult to get funding for back cataloging materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: It is not, as they say, the sexiest thing to ask for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: A lot of things around our collection care description are among the more challenging things for us to get funding for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The digitization question is a really interesting one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: The library has a digital collections portal that is accessible online that has a little bit over a million items.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so if you do the math out of our 55 million, you can see that that's actually a relatively small portion of our materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We're very thoughtful about how we digitize materials because there's a balance that we seek through this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We want to make sure that our collections are accessible globally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: whenever we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: It costs a lot of money to come, if you don't live in New York, to do research at a place like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And if somebody is writing about any one of our collections, we want to make sure that there is not a cost prohibition for them to come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: At the same time, we believe very strongly in our in-person operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We believe very strongly that we want to support people coming to the library, which is why we spend hundreds of thousands of dollars a year on research fellowships so that people can come and have that remarkable experience of having materials accessible

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: in our reading room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We're also limited by copyright law and the materials that we are able to put online for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so for that reason, you know, we think very, very carefully about the things that we do digitize because we want to make sure if we are digitizing that we can make them widely available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We're happy to get back to you with more numbers and the details.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And I just want to add that was mentioned in the introduction that the Library for the Performing Arts just got this incredible gift of $60 million, the largest gift in the Performing Arts Library history by an anonymous donor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And all of that is going to, we're going to engage in the next five years in actually a program to digitize a lot more of our collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And so the idea is actually also to make that available to anyone and also improve the experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So I think in the next five years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: Julie mentioned we have about over a million items digitized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We're going to see that number go up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And it will focus on items from the Library for Performing Arts collection, but we're going to set up systems that are going to be available to all the different research libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So I think we will see that number increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: But also, as Julie said, I think the in-person experience is also very special, so it's important to look at both of these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I'm starting to feel a way about the $60 million, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So for Langston Hughes specifically, we are a smaller collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So for us, we prioritize digitizing anything that was deteriorating, which for us was VHSs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So the majority of our VHS collection has been digitized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And as far as our central library, we would say about 15 to 20% of our materials have been digitized, and about 70% is cataloged and accessible under our Queens Archive program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have specific numbers for digitization, but I can always find that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: The majority of our archival collections are at least minimally processed, so people can see descriptions of those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We tend to digitize materials that are fragile, that are not easy to be used, so that we can provide greater access to our patrons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We also tend to prioritize collections that are at risk of obsolescence, so analog, audio tape and video tape and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We rely, of course, on grant funding to be able to digitize those materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Another thing that we do, because we do realize how important it is to have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: more materials be available online is that we've created workflows within ourselves and within our department to add materials that we digitize for patron requests to our digital collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So whatever we do ourselves, we are able to create metadata and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: build on our collection in that way rather than waiting for funding for a larger collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So just little ways that help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We really try to do that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks who decides what the library acquires, whether they have a written collecting policy, and how community members inform those decisions. Joy Bivens, Natiba Guy-Clement, and Shakira Smalls describe their collection development policies and community input.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson asks about acquisition policy; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I have one more question, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Who decides what the library acquires?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have a written collecting policy?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How often is it revised and how do community members, scholars, librarians, and archivists inform those decisions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: The New York Public Library does have a collecting policy in terms, and that is broad for all of our research centers, but what each research center

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: collects is based on the mission and focus of that particular center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And then it's not revised like every five years where we're like, these five years we're going to collect this or that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We really do engage the gaps in our collections, in our holdings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: We really do listen to the researchers who are engaging our collections to understand what they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And for instance, the Schomburg has instituted an initiative called the Next Century of Black Studies because we want to hear from

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Black studies professors, researchers, what is it that they need to write the scholarship of the next century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And so utilizing that, we not only are thinking about what we collect, but also what we process and what we digitize and make available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So I would say that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Globally, the library has a very specific collecting policy, but locally we are each determining

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: What are the needs of our particular holdings?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Yeah, so similar to what Joy is saying regarding we do rely a lot on our researcher questions and requests, as well as those of our students and the teachers that we work with in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do have a collection development policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It is online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Anyone can read it and access it and see what our priorities are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I am trying to revise mine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: This is my 50th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So that is a project for us going into next year because we do want to keep it current because things change so quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And when we first created that policy was when we started a CBH.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So a lot has happened over the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that our policy is in line with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And who helps us to make acquisition decisions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a committee that comprises of professors, historians, long-term Brooklynites that helps us to make collecting decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Queens is very similar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Langston Hughes specifically, we do abide by a policy that we are grateful has been completely relevant for the last 40 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So there's little to updating that's necessarily for the Black Heritage Reference Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: As far as for our central library, our central archives,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: Acquisition policy is geared towards related to geographic of Long Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So they work with families and organizations to acquire items and represent the history of the borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And similarly to all of our reference collection, we have a devoted team that's responsible for overseeing and making the decision of what should be added to the collection.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all, and thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry asks about capital funding lead times for library projects. Julie Golia, Roberta Pineda, Natiba Guy-Clement, Joy Bivens, and Julie Golia discuss the complexities of the capital process and the need for reform.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks about capital funding lead times; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to piggyback off one of your finance questions.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I can remember starting a couple of months ago and speaking to QL, Queens Public Library leadership, and we were talking about capital.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They had all these amazing capital projects to be funded and said,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This is what we need.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We're going to tell you now it won't start for seven years.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I only have an eight year term.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So my question to you all is, when you're trying to expand your collections, when you're trying to make improvements, how does, one, I know what the lead time for Queens is.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is it the same lead time across the city?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how do you plan for that, prepare for that, and how can we do better by you in the city to expedite the process?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Can you clarify, do you mean in terms of the collecting that we're doing or in terms of broader?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Capital funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Broader capital funding.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Broader capital funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: I will say that one of the challenging parts of this job is that we are in the business of forever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We are collecting this material and we are safeguarding it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: This is not our material, we're just holding it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And so, as we were even mentioning before with all these climate concerns, it becomes really important to have good capital infrastructure, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And so,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: A lot of that is very complicated, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: You know, you're looking at some money to fix a roof or something, and then you understand that that's going to take many years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: What do you do until then?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So I think that, to answer your question, yes, if the systems were a little bit less complicated and we could get these important capital upgrades

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: done faster, I think this would actually make all our collections safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It's the same process for us at BPL as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Of course, we try to expedite things as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I think we also have the added challenge at CBH of being a landmark building with a landmark interior library, which, beautiful to look at, but, you know, it...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: The building was built in 1881, and there's a lot more stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we really try to think creatively in terms of how we manage collection storage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do off-site storage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do try to limit the amount of time it takes to get materials to our researchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: But of course, yeah, any funding to help that, of course, we'll all appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: You're looking at me, so I think I'm supposed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because you have such a beautiful space here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Yes, it is beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And we are about to embark on a facade project to replace all of the windows for this particular building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And it has...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Taken many, many years to get to the point of starting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And, you know, there's contractors, there's contracts, there are issues around, this is not the landmark building, but we do have a landmark building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So I'm not sure, I think the funding is one thing, then there's the kind of machinations and process of actually

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: either city or state contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: So I'm not sure how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: It has taken many years, really.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I think we are so grateful for the council's support, and I think the council knows that we have worked

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: for a while on the challenges around the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I think the challenges very much have to do with the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And I think as Roberta says, in the meantime, we are preserving, in the case of the law,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: 55 million collection items that we are on the hook for maintaining forever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: So I think we are really eager to work with you and support any ways to reform the complexities of the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We all get it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We work at bureaucratic places as well, so we get it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: But this would...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Greatly help us be better and more responsible stewards to preserving these collections for future children, generations of the people that we are doing this for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And in the meantime, we try to work around the capital process in any way that we can, which is not an ideal situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: So we really look forward to more conversations on how we can refine that process.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry gives a point of privilege to praise the Langston Hughes Library and Cultural Center in her district. She shares personal memories and highlights its role as a cultural institution and the largest Black history reading collection in NYC.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry praises Langston Hughes Library

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'm open in all ears.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Chair, if I can take a point of privilege.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My next thing is a comment.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I am a Queens girl through and through.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So Queens Public Library is my library.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have four branches in my district.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But I have to say my favorite is the Langston Hughes Library and Cultural Center.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Over 55 years in the community, and I don't know if you heard it when Shakira testified, but the largest, the largest black history reading collection in all of New York City is housed at Langston Hughes Library and Cultural Center.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So, Chair, when you ask about how do people learn about them, I'm going to just tell everybody in this room how you're going to learn about Langston Hughes and the cultures in my district.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If I can for a second, you open the door.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Over 55 years, and this is not just a library, this is a cultural institution.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want you to understand it didn't start as a library.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It started as neighbors getting together to build something during the civil rights movement and Black Panther era when our communities were poverty stricken and no one wanted to invest.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And it was neighbors and individuals, some of those neighbors and individuals who serve on that board today who are in this room that built this library over 55 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This is a library where I walked my kindergarten graduation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I could speak, say my numbers from one to ten in at least five different languages, one of them being Swahili.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Swahili.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And this was 40 plus years ago.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And 40 plus years later, that same librarian who taught me now watches and helps teach my children today.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So again, this is a cultural institution in the community of Corona East Umhurst, the 21st Council District.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Also the home of the Langston.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: of the Louis Armstrong House and Museum.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So when we talk about history, Corona has built history.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It is part of history.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It was where Martin Luther King interned.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It was where the famous Malcolm X house that was bombed is today.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It was where Harry Belafonte once called home.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It was where our great former assemblyman, Jefferyon Arbery, advocated to repeal the Rockefeller drug laws.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
