utterances.text: It is where the first black president of Queensborough, Helen Marshall Hale from, who held this council seat.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So when you want to know where to go to learn about some history, come to my district in Corona and visit the Langston Hughes Cultural Center and the Louis Armstrong House and Museum.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because one thing that a lot of these collection house, the Louis Armstrong Center just finished the Corona collection, where individuals who grew up on the block with Louis.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Louis taught these young people as children how to play the trumpet, are able to tell those stories.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So when we talk about capital investments taking too long, we don't have too long for those stories to be told the way that they're told in these institutions.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I give back my time and say thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks whether the research centers are designed truly for the public or if they see more use from scholars and researchers. Julie Golia, Roberta Pineda, and Natiba Guy-Clement discuss efforts to make spaces welcoming and the challenges of historic buildings.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about accessibility; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just two more questions and then we're going to go to Zoom and then come back.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I know that you all did mention how much you work really hard to make your spaces accessible to the general public.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: public, but just wanted to get a better sense of whether or not you feel that these sensors are designed truly for the public, or do you see more use for scholars and researchers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I just want to share that Nativa and I gave each other a look just now because we both work in buildings that were built over 100 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: When libraries...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Like research libraries, we're not necessarily designed to be the welcoming open spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: People often say, oh, you're so lucky to work at that building with the lions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: But sometimes I look across the street at our new Stavros Niarchos Foundation Library with a little bit of jealousy because it's incredibly welcoming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: There are plugs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: There's low-hanging seating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: There's children's books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: It feels remarkably welcoming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We are proud of our old buildings and our architecture, but they can be a real challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I have a very vivid memory myself as a researcher going into the New York Public Library and feeling incredibly intimidated by that building, not feeling like it was for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And I think that many of my coworkers share that experience, and we work every day to break down those walls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: At 42nd Street, we've recently launched a new welcome philosophy where we invite new users in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We look to transform first-time visitors into researchers by giving them

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: a hospitality-infused experience of public service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We want to meet people where they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We don't want to say, what are you doing here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We want to say, how can we help you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And we've looked at everything from restaurant services to hotels to hospitals as examples of ways that we can serve people better and more intuitively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: But we still struggle, I would say, with our architecture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so we look for ways through signage, through programming, and I think most importantly, you'll have heard across this panel, reaching people at the youngest age possible is what transforms people into regular library users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: So it's great to say it to somebody when they're 30 or 35.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: If we can get them when they're 7 or 14 or when they first arrive at college, we have an opportunity to transform a young person's worldview

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: about our building and for them to come into the grandness of our building and not say, I'm intimidated, but say, this was built for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And I just wanted to add, too, the Library for the Performing Arts, we're a little bit different because beyond being a research library, we're also a circulating neighborhood library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So you can actually come in at any time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: You can pick up your holds from anywhere from New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: We have this beautiful first floor lounge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: If you go there, especially after school, you see some teenagers doing TikTok dances, some people doing Zoom meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: You see a little bit of everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: And I think for us, what we are working on now is to get these casual library users that might just be there using the library as a third space to engage with our collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So how do we get those students doing a TikTok dance to go up to our third floor and see this beautiful video of Baryshnikov doing a dance, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: How do we get the people that were just in a Zoom meeting to come visit our exhibitions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: So this is the work that we are doing now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Roberta Pineda
utterances.text: But in terms of the space, as I said, it's a very welcoming, just like any of our neighborhood libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Yeah, so, I mean, our building is extremely intimidating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: It's something that we try to address every single day, and we really have cultivated a kind of ethos of being of welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We put aside space in our library for people who are just doing their own work, so it's not like we're, you know, you are not doing research, you can't come in here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: No, we understand it's a beautiful space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: People want to be there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: People get inspired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I love it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: They come in, they do their work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: And like I said earlier, eventually we hope that they do research with us, but they know that it's a space that they can be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: What Julie mentioned, bringing children in at a very young age so that they understand like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: archival collections, I can touch these, it's fine for me to use them, and I can also be in the space and be, you know, feel welcomed and everyone is really happy that I'm here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We do a lot of work with even signage in our building because a lot of people come in and they're like, what is this place?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Or they come to the library and they're like, I didn't know that this place existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So we really try to welcome every single person that comes in through our doors downstairs in our library on the second floor and really give them an experience that they want to come back.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks whether staffing in the research centers is sufficient and what credentials the staff have. Natiba Guy-Clement, Julie Golia, and Shakira Smalls describe their teams, including archivists, librarians, catalogers, and the page program.
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks about staffing; library directors respond

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Final question is just about staffing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know, I'm sure the answer is never enough, but is staffing in these centers and collections sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If anything has changed over the past 10 years, would be good to know that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And if you could just tell us about who the staff are in the centers and collections and what are their credentials.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know this is not typical library, so you might have other specialty staff working on your teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: Since my mic is closest, I can get started.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: So at Center for Brooklyn History, we have a team of archivists, reference librarians, special collections catalogers, art and artifact coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a library page because we want to make sure that we give students who are in library school an opportunity to have a paid job while also learning about what a library is and how it functions, especially in a research space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a wonderful team of educators who go out into Brooklyn schools and manage field trips.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a director of programs who does all of our wonderful public programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: We have a chief historian who is in the audience today who is wonderful and does all of our public history and exhibitions work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I think that might be it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Natiba Guy-Clement
utterances.text: I hope I'm not missing anyone, but a very varied staff.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, and if there are any other different types of staffers that she did not mention, because that seems like a very robust list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I want to add that NYPL is a really big place, and so one group of people who often get kind of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: not seen as much are the teams that we call the technical services teams, the people who preserve the collections, who describe the collections, who catalog the collections, the people who make sure that they're in the right place on the shelf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We have, you know, in the 42nd Street building, for example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We have seven miles of archival shelving, and every single box on one of those is coded properly in a database so that we can find it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: If one of those goes in the wrong place, we lose track of that box, and that is a remarkable labor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We also have curators, and I think this is a really important thing to think about, people who not just preserve the collections and steward the collections, but interpret the collections, who bring them to life for people through exhibitions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And then the one thing I want to flag about our library, which Nativa is a great representative of, is we have so many people who start as pages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Our page program is robust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: We get students from all across both graduate school and undergraduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And we are incredibly proud of the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: I just talked to one of our colleagues here at the Schomburg this morning who started as a page and made his way up into management here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: And so the library is really committed to growing our staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Lots of people understand that librarians are a part of this, but we support almost every kind of career path just at the New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: I won't be too repetitive, but for Queens Public Library, when we say curators, archivists, we have one person for each research collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So for example, at Langston Hughes Library with the Black Heritage Reference Center, there is one person taking care of a 40,000 plus collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: We have one music librarian that's taking care of 40,000 music records and documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So when my colleagues were talking, they were saying things like archivists and curators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: And I'm like, yeah, we have one for that collection and one for another collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shakira Smalls
utterances.text: So I just wanted to add that.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams asks if there is anything else the panel wants to share or anything the council can do outside of funding. Joy Bivens responds simply: 'Come visit us. And tell people about us.'
chapters.title: Chair Williams asks for final comments; Joy Bivens responds

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think that you all provided such robust testimony.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't know if there's anything else that you wanted to share or if there is anything that the council can do outside of funding to support your centers and collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Come visit us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joy Bivens
utterances.text: And tell people about us.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks the library panel and announces that the committee will now hear from individuals joining from Puerto Rico on Zoom. Maria del Mar Rosa-Rodriguez introduces herself as a professor at the University of Puerto Rico and president of the Puerto Rican Association of University Professors.
chapters.title: Chair moves to Puerto Rico Zoom panel; Maria del Mar Rosa-Rodriguez introduces herself

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We are not done.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We know we have more folks testifying from the libraries, but as I signaled earlier, we are going to continue to walk and chew gum at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And we have some individuals zooming in from Puerto Rico, and we want to get to them at this time.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we are going to hear from Professor Maria Del Marosa.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Christina Miranda Palacios and Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Segui.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Segui.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, I got to pronounce this correctly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Rosa Segui.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Did I start?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, you can start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So first of all, thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: My name is Maria del Mar Rosa Rodriguez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: I am a professor at the University of Puerto Rico and the president of the APU, the Puerto Rican Association of University Professors, the faculty union here at the UBR.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: I represent more than 3,000 academics, and I want to tell our story, right?

chapters.summary: Rosa-Rodriguez describes the University of Puerto Rico as the only public university in the archipelago, with 11 campuses. She notes that 75% of all research in Puerto Rico happens at the UPR and that it is the main provider of health services.
chapters.title: Rosa-Rodriguez discusses UPR's role and value

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So my story is the story of many in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: I am an alumni of the University of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: My parents were first-generation college graduates, thanks to the UPR.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: The UPR gave my brother and I, my cousins, my neighbors, a way out of poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So the UPR has 11 campuses that guarantee access to education throughout Puerto Rico as the only public university in the archipelago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: It has the highest retention and graduation rates, but the UPR is so much more than an academic institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: The UPR sustains our country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Studies have shown that for every dollar invested in the university, there is a return of 1.5.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: 75% of all research that comes out of Puerto Rico happens in the university.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: It's also the main provider of health services in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: It's the biggest agricultural program with experimental stations and an outreach service to communities as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: And I could go on and on listing all the ways in which the UPR is essential for us.

chapters.summary: Rosa-Rodriguez says the UPR has suffered unsustainable budget cuts since La Junta arrived in 2016. She argues La Junta acts above the law and supports Resolution 28 to end the fiscal oversight board.
chapters.title: Rosa-Rodriguez discusses La Junta's cuts and supports Resolution 28

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So if the UPR is all this, why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Then why is it the main target of La Junta, of the Federal Oversight Management Board?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Since their arrival in 2016, the UPR has suffered unsustainable budget cuts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: La Junta acts above the law, avoiding Puerto Rican laws that invest in the university.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: We now have less than half of the budget that we should have because of the financial oversight of La Junta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: The Junta has exceeded their financial oversight and are demanding structural, labor, educational, and ideological changes that are not in their purview.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So why dismantle one of the main institutions that can generate economic growth, social mobility, community outreach, access to the best health services in the country, and accessible education for our future generations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Well, the answer is clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Life is not at the center of the agenda of La Junta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Debt and austerity are because they respond to capital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: They go above state law and take without permission and without accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Puerto Rico is a good land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: laboratory for this anti-democratic experiment that if successful can be reproduced in the states when they need to answer to big capital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: So there are plenty of reasons from Puerto Rico and from the states to call on the United States Congress to end the financial oversight and management board for Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: The faculty of the University of Puerto Rico supports the resolution 28 2026 to end la junta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - María del Mar Rosa-Rodríguez
utterances.text: Thanks for listening and thanks for the opportunity.

chapters.summary: Cristina Miranda Palacios introduces herself as founding executive director of La Liga de Ciudades de Puerto Rico. She supports all four resolutions and describes her organization's vision of a municipalist Puerto Rico.
chapters.title: Cristina Miranda Palacios introduces herself

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Christina?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Hola.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Members of the New York City Council, buenas tardes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: My name is Cristina Miranda Palacios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: I'm the founding executive director of La Liga de Ciudades de Puerto Rico, nonpartisan organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Our North Star is a municipalist Puerto Rico, a country that governs from the ground up, where municipalities are the foundation of democratic life and their municipal governments are the engine of the people's well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: It is from that vision that we support all four resolutions before you today.

chapters.summary: Miranda Palacios says PROMESA was a perverse imposition and supports ending the board. She explains that eliminating the equalization fund would leave 43 of 78 municipalities with budget cuts of 30-60%, rendering them fiscally unviable.
chapters.title: Miranda Palacios discusses Resolution 28 and municipal impact

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: On Resolution 28, we are in full support of ending what should never have existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Promesa was, from its origin, a perverse imposition, and 10 years in, their most tangible result is that Puerto Rico, Puerto Ricans, and our communities have been robbed of a decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: It must end now, and reparations must follow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: When the board eliminated the primary fund for municipalities, the equalization fund, it promised a substitute mechanism, and it never created one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: La Liga's own analysis found that the elimination of this fund would leave 43 out of our 78 units of municipal government with budget cuts of 30 to 60 percent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: rendering them fiscally unviable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: They have not collapsed because of a life preserver made of ice that is rapidly melting, as U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Government funds assigned for the post-disaster recuperation of Puerto Rico have an end date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Hear me when I say this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: The provider of essential services, the units of municipal government,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: will disappear, but the need will not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Puerto Rico is not vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: We have been made vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: And resolutions like the ones discussed today help us fight back.

chapters.summary: Miranda Palacios expresses support for Resolution 372 to repeal Act 22, Resolution 27 to stop predatory debt practices, and Resolution 494 to stop Project Esencia. She concludes with 'Puerto Rico ni se vende ni se regala.'
chapters.title: Miranda Palacios supports other resolutions and concludes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: We fully support Resolution 372 repealing Act 22 to ensure a Puerto Rico paso gente.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Resolution 27 to stop the illegal dip practices that continue to extract and weaken our nation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: And Resolution 494 to stop Project Esencia porque Esencia no va.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: As New York knows well, what happens aquí in Puerto Rico is a preview of what will happen allá.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Because connecting our municipalities with New York City to share strategies and solutions is more vital than ever, I urge you to pass these four resolutions on behalf of Puerto Rico, on behalf of justice, and on behalf of the power of lo posible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Puerto Rico ni se vende ni se regala.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristina Miranda Palacios
utterances.text: Gracias.

chapters.summary: Rosa Segui Cordero introduces herself as a spokesperson for the Movimiento Victoria Ciudadana. She expresses support for Resolutions 27, 28, 372, and 494.
chapters.title: Rosa Segui Cordero introduces herself

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And last but not least for now is Rosa Seguin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: To all the members of the New York City Council, I am Rosa Segui Cordero and appear before you as a spokesperson for the Movimiento Victoria Ciudadana.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: We thank the opportunity and fully support resolutions number 27, 28,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: 372 and 494 of 2026, all before the Committee of Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations.

chapters.summary: Segui Cordero notes that this year marks 10 years since PROMESA imposed the Financial Oversight and Management Board. She criticizes the board for exercising authoritarian control, cutting essential services, and prioritizing payments to vulture funds.
chapters.title: Segui Cordero discusses PROMESA and La Junta

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: We begin by noting that this year marks the decade, 10 long years during which Puerto Rico has been subjected to an unprecedented colonial legal framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Under the territorial clause of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Constitution, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Congress passed the Promesa Act in 2016, using that law to impose the Financial Oversight and Management Board, or La Junta de Control Fiscal, as we refer to it in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: For 10 long years, our people have been subjected to the unilateral and authoritarian control of the board, exercising power akin to that of a military regime,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: which without local expertise decides how much of our people's money is allocated to education, essential services, public safety,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: and housing, but largely how much of it is cut to hand over to vulture funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: The board also has struck down legislation passed by the democratically elected

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Legislative Assembly of Puerto Rico and signed by the executive branch, violating the democratic principle of the consent of the governed and representing significant setbacks in the protection of our human and civil rights, as you have heard before me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Because of the board, we stumble upon one crisis to the next to pay off an unpayable, odious, and illegal colonial debt owed to Montalbillion dollar voter funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Because of the board, daily life in Puerto Rico is extremely difficult due to the impact of austerity measures that they have imposed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Puerto Ricans know all too well the human impact of repaying abusive debts and the predatory practices of vulture funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: That is why we support Resolution 28, because New York, as the United Nations has already stated, must stop enabling and abetting these investment practices that are harming the entire world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: We are continuously forced to endure it all, from power outages to crisis, regarding access to potable water, all due to the lack of public investment caused by the board.

chapters.summary: Segui Cordero opposes Project Esencia for its environmental and community impacts. She also supports repealing Act 22, noting that more than $20 billion in funds are lost due to tax privileges for the wealthy.
chapters.title: Segui Cordero discusses Project Esencia and Act 22

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Victoria Ciudadana also joins the widespread opposition to the development of the Proyecto Esencia off the coast of Cabo Rojo, as it represents a direct assault on the environment and the quality of life of our southwestern region.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: That is why we support Resolution 494 and call upon this Council to join the voices of the people of Puerto Rico opposing this type of neocolonial extractive project,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: one that seeks only to displace local residents under the guise of economic development, a narrative that we have been time and time again promoted, resulting in prosperity for the few while extracting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: profits from our people and displacing our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Finally, and no less importantly, if we want to prevent Puerto Rico from continuing to cycle through economic and debt crisis and lack of access to water and energy, and instead provide the Puerto Rican people with a country where they are truly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: alive in well-being, where they truly live in well-being, we must stop turning our archipelago into a fiscal paradise for investors at the expense of our people and natural resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: More than $20 billion in funds are being lost due to these tax privileges for the wealthy, while the people of Puerto Rico struggle to survive amidst shortages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: That is why we also support Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: 376, calling on the government of Puerto Rico to sign legislation, and finally, we appeal Act 22.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: We strongly urge the Council to pass these resolutions and stand with us in solidarity without erasure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosa Seguí Cordero
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams introduces former City Council Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito. Mark-Viverito introduces herself as a former speaker born and raised in Puerto Rico and a member of the diaspora.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Melissa Mark-Viverito; Mark-Viverito introduces herself

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, and I love the books and your background, very apropos, we are at a library.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And with that, we do have a special guest in person, the first Latina Puerto Rican former speaker, Melissa Mark-Viverito, to provide testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody, council members and chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Wonderful to see you all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: And incredibly powerful that this conversation is happening here at the Arturo Schomburg Research Center, all that he represents to us in the diaspora and in Puerto Rico and as Boricuas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: So good afternoon, gracias for holding this important hearing today on resolutions 294, 27, 28, and 372.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: I am Melissa Marguerito, former city council speaker, born and raised in Puerto Rico as a colonial subject.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: I'm before you today, a member of our extensive diaspora, using my voice and leveraging my actions to demand my island's sovereignty.

chapters.summary: Mark-Viverito quotes Barbados Prime Minister Mia Motley on the underdevelopment of Africa, the Caribbean, and Latin America as a child of the colonial experiment. She says Puerto Rico has not yet freed itself from that experiment.
chapters.title: Mark-Viverito quotes Mia Motley on colonialism

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: I would like to start by sharing a quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: We have to understand that the underdevelopment of Africa, of the Caribbean, of Latin America, in many instances, is a child.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: of the colonial experiment, and the colonial experiment extracted wealth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: And in some of these countries, the extractive attitudes still remain, such that we haven't been able to build the kind of domestic enterprises and the domestic foundations that's necessary to sustain our people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: This quote from Barbados Prime Minister Mia Motley speaks to Puerto Rico's reality today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: We have not yet freed ourselves from that colonial experiment, but it is a moral imperative that we do so, that it is Puerto Rico who has the ability to build that domestic foundation necessary to sustain our people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: The resolutions in discussion today speak to a scourge that must be uprooted, the continued economic and political subjugation of Puerto Rico and its people.

chapters.summary: Mark-Viverito says the resolutions are interwoven by extractive settler colonialism. She connects Act 22 to displacement and overdevelopment, Project Esencia to environmental destruction, and La Junta to anti-democratic control.
chapters.title: Mark-Viverito discusses interwoven resolutions and extractive colonialism

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: These individual resolutions are deeply interwoven, as some of the speakers have indicated, by one common thread, extractive settler colonialism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Individuals opting to relocate to Puerto Rico to evade federal, state, and local taxes via Act 22 are bringing with them displacement, increased cost of living, and overdevelopment, thereby paving the way for projects like Essencia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: And projects like Essencia subsequently extract economic wealth via the destruction of Puerto Rico's environmental wealth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: This development, if allowed to be fulfilled, will cause unmanageable devastation and will open the door to other similar devastation across the island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Finally, an anti-democracy construct in Puerto

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: by Congress, La Junta, reinforces the view that as a colonized people, Puerto Rico should not have agency over its future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Constructs such as these must be abolished and La Junta must end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: And that is why these resolutions are important, because they are a statement of values in support of sovereignty and against the rapacious and corrupt systems that perpetuate economic insecurity by destroying the ability for economic self-sufficiency.

chapters.summary: Mark-Viverito quotes bell hooks: 'What we can't imagine can't come to be.' She imagines a self-sufficient, thriving Puerto Rico and calls on the council to pass the resolutions as a statement of values.
chapters.title: Mark-Viverito concludes with bell hooks quote and call to action

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: What we can't imagine can't come to be is a bell hooks quote I recently came across.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Every day, I imagine a self-sufficient Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Every day, I imagine a Puerto Rico thriving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: A Puerto Rico where my mother and eventually I can age with dignity, and every day I imagine un Puerto Rico libre.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: I only hope that it is within my lifetime that our collective imagining will fully realize our eventual liberation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Gracias for your time today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Gracias for the moral values expressed via these resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: By speaking up for Puerto Ricans on the island, this city council is defending New Yorkers, not just Boricuas, but also everyone who has faced gentrification,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: environmental and health degradation, and exploitation by elites who think their wealth is worth more than the democratic power of our collective will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Let these resolutions send a message from San Juan to Washington and serve as a framework for other legislatures to follow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Mark-Viverito
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks Mark-Viverito and officially opens public testimony. She reminds the public of decorum rules and calls the first panel of Queens folks: Wendy, Jason, Regina, and Joette.
chapters.title: Chair Williams opens public testimony and calls first panel

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thanks, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, I just want to

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Say, what am I supposed to exactly read here?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We haven't received a public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Give us a second.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, so I do feel like we've already been hearing public testimony, but we'll officially open it up to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I want to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms if you have not already done so and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's topic, examining the research collections of New York City's public libraries, or on the resolutions we are hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I will now call the first panel from the public, which will be a panel of Queens folks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we'll start with Wendy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Charania, Jason, our Queens historian, who I was honored with.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The other day at King Manor, and Regina from the Louis.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Armstrong House Museum.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, and another, Joette John from Queens Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't know if Joette John is here.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We can start.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Maybe we want to start with our historian.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Please.

chapters.summary: Jason Antos, Queensborough historian, testifies about his experience using the Queens Library archives since age 19. He advocates for continued support of local history research collections.
chapters.title: Jason Antos testifies on Queens history and libraries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: Hi, good to see you again.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Good to see you too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: So to the New York City Council, my name is Jason Antos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: I am the current Queensborough historian.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: I'm also the director at the Queens Historical Society in Flushing, and I'm just here to talk as an advocate for the research and collection of local history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: Via the public library system, specifically the Queens Library system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: I had been using the central, or what used to be known as the Long Island Division, now known as the Archives at the Central Library, since I'm 19 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: I started off researching Queens history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: As a hobby and eventually turned into a part-time job and now as a career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: And had it not been for the Queens Library,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: and the other library branches of the greater city of New York probably wouldn't have been to this level that I am now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: In fact, Queens history is everywhere, and it covers all of the other library systems as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: It includes the New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: It includes the Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: In fact, on my social media, about two months ago, I visited the Center for Brooklyn History, and I put under the caption, what is the Queensborough historian doing in Brooklyn?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: And that's to say that the collections in these archives are tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: And they do a huge public service to the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: And I just came down here today to advocate for their continued support because I'm living proof that if you go down there as a young researcher and you dedicate your time and your life to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: these places into these wonderful institutions that can lead you down a very good path in life and that they provide a tremendous service to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Antos
utterances.text: And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Golia
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wendy Pellot, co-vice chair of the Library Action Committee, testifies about growing up near the Langston Hughes Community Library. She highlights its role as a community hub and its circulating Black heritage collection.
chapters.title: Wendy Pellot testifies on Langston Hughes Library

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Pellot
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Pellot
utterances.text: My name is Wendy Pettis, and I'd like to say good morning, members of the committee and fellow New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Pellot
utterances.text: I love libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Pellot
utterances.text: I have library cards from QPL, BPL, and NYPL, and I was in Brooklyn yesterday and walked over to the Grand Army Plaza Library in the rain just to gaze at those beautiful doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Pellot
utterances.text: The Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center is my home library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I grew up just two blocks away, born in 1969, like the library, the very same year local grassroots organizers fought to build it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Today, as co-vice chair of the Library Action Committee, which supports the library, I see its power firsthand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It's far more than a library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It's a thriving community hub.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Week after week, residents gather here for cultural events, critical conversations, and local organizing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In addition to having research archives like the Schomburg, Langston Hughes also houses New York City's largest circulating black heritage collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Growing up, I didn't just study history behind glass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I checked those books and videos and carried them home out of just curiosity and for my advanced studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Today, over 40,000 pieces can go directly into the hands and backpacks of neighborhood families and anyone else with a library card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: To invest in Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center is to protect living history, community activism, and neighborhood literacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It shaped my life and empowers our community every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Regina Bain, director of the Louis Armstrong House Museum, testifies about the museum's 60,000-piece Armstrong archive. She emphasizes the importance of preserving and sharing collections for future generations.
chapters.title: Regina Bain testifies on Louis Armstrong House Museum

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Hello, I'm Regina Bain, director of the Louis Armstrong House Museum in Corona, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: It's a pleasure to be here at the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: I grew up in libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: We love libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: And we are thankful for the partnerships of the public libraries, including Queens Public Library, including Langston Hughes, that have provided in the programs that help serve our shared communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: The museum is the steward of the 13 collection, 60,000 piece Armstrong archive, the largest of any single jazz musician, for many years housed at Queens College

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: and now housed at the Armstrong Center on 107th Street, right across the street from the historic landmark house.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: The Armstrong personal library of books that were in their home when they died are a prominent part of our collections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: The books from their personal library that are currently featured in our exhibition include Roots by Alex Haley, The Black Book edited by Toni Morrison, and I Speak of Freedom by Kwame Nkrumah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Our programming in the next months when we open the Armstrong in Ghana exhibition includes a public reading of the book Black Star in the Wind by Robert Raymond, chronicling Armstrong's trip to Ghana in 1956

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: in the midst of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Civil Rights Movement and the Ghanaian independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: As an organization whose mission is ensuring the Armstrong legacy and the values therein endure,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: we know the importance of preserving and sharing collections so those who come after us can look at the information with their own eyes, discover connections with their own experiences, and come to their own conclusions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: based on the facts available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Louis Armstrong knew, and we know, that is how stories survive, and that is how legacies continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sharanya Ramakrishnan, director of the Corona Collection and Oral History Project, testifies about documenting the lives of neighbors who knew Louis and Lucille Armstrong. She highlights partnerships with Queens Public Library and the Langston Hughes Community Library.
chapters.title: Sharanya Ramakrishnan testifies on Corona Collection

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the Honorable Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: I'm Sharanya Ramakrishnan, Director of Community Engagement at the Louis Armstrong House Museum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: I'm also the Director of the Corona Collection and Oral History Project that documents the lives and stories of neighbors who personally knew Louis and Lucille Armstrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: This important project helps preserve our collective memory while creating an intergenerational legacy of the community and the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Central to this project is the in-depth research of the archives and collections preserved by libraries, especially those of the Black Heritage Reference Center at the Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: and the digital archives at the Central Branch of Queens Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Our work also extends beyond preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Through our partnership with the Queen's Library Jail and Prison Outreach Program, we bring live jazz performances and the legacy of Louis Armstrong to the Queensborough Correctional Facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: We also collaborated with the Langston Hughes Community Library and the Library Action Committee and other community organizations to organize a walking tour,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Roots and Rhythm, supported by the council member Chanel Thomas-Henry's office that uplifts the history, the deep history of Corona and East Elmhurst neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: These efforts reflect that libraries are not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: not simply repositories of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: They are living institutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: They are part of the ecosystem of consciousness, of the social and cultural lives of communities and neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Libraries are also a space for people to access essential services, participate in public programs and build skills,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Therefore, investment in libraries is an investment in the cultural and civic life of New York City, and strengthening libraries and cultural institutions is essential in building an equitable pathway for the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharanya Ramakrishnan
utterances.text: Williams and the entire committee for this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wyatt John, a senior at Thomas A. Edison CTE High School, testifies about his experience in the Sankofa series at Langston Hughes Library. He describes studying Black history and teaching younger students what he learned.
chapters.title: Wyatt John testifies on Sankofa series

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: My name is Wyatt John, and I'm a senior at Thomas A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: Edison CTE High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: This summer, I was one of the 13 people in the Sankofa series, Legacy Forward at the Langston Hughes Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: Sankofa means go back and get it, and that's exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: We studied Black Wall Street, Black inventors, Black voices in film and media, and our roots and identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: We sat across from a Black Panther veteran, a Vietnam veteran, and an executive producer, and asked our own questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: A moment that stayed with me was hearing firsthand from a Black Panther veteran and realizing that the history we read about in textbooks is still alive and real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: And carried by people right here in our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: We found those stories in the Black Heritage Reference Center, in books, newspapers, and history we could actually hold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: As a final project, we taught first through eighth graders what we learned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: That's what a research collection does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: It doesn't just keep history, it passes it forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: Please keep investing in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wyatt John
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks the panel and asks Wyatt John how he found out about the Sankofa program at Langston Hughes. She appreciates his testimony.
chapters.title: Chair Williams thanks panel and asks Wyatt about program

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't think we have any more questions for this panel, but I appreciate you so much for coming and testifying, especially our young person who's going to school at Thomas Edison.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's amazing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Right outside of my district.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Not my district, but right outside of my district.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But where do you live?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you live in Corona?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, okay, Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All right, thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Actually, I do have a question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How did you find out about that program at Langston Hughes?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Awesome, thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams calls the NYPL panel. Jasson Daniels testifies about his experience in the Junior Scholars program at the Schomburg Center, which influenced his career as a writer and producer.
chapters.title: Chair calls NYPL panel; Jasson Daniels testifies on Junior Scholars

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, we are gonna move on to a panel from New York Public Libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Bill Goldstein, Brent Edwards, Key Choi, and Jalen Daniels.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And Jacqueline, is this the same?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: This looks like the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh no, two different Daniels.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Jaylen and Jacqueline Daniels.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Jacqueline.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Jocelyn.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Jocelyn.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Whoever wants to start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: I can go first.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, no worries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Good afternoon, city council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: My name is Jasson Daniels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: In 2015, my sister and I walked through these halls for the first time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Even the mere presence of the same floors that Toni Morrison, Langston Hughes, Nella Larson, Zora Neale Hurston, and so many more have danced through made a significant impact on my psyche.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Being accepted into and chosen for a program like the Junior Scholars felt prestigious and allowed me to explore interests like spoken word, theater, and film,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: all of which influences my calling of becoming a writer and producer today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: I remember I messed up the poem I had memorized for my first ever showcase, stuttering in silence, but it didn't matter because the show went on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: I was able to make a mistake and survive it in this building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Outside these walls, however, I attended a predominantly white institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Many of the other students showed clear political affiliation to the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: billionaire bigot America elected in 2016.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: And the school also ended up enrolling our current president's child.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Safe to say I needed a third space like the Schomburg to find refuge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: I believe in the power of storytelling and preserving that power, especially in the age of AI,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: where we soon might not be able to discern reality from fantasy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: This is what the Schomburg Center and the Junior Scholars can do for black children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Give them the history and the tools to discern and discover hidden truths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jasson Daniels
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jaylen Daniels, Jasson's sister and a Junior Scholars alumna, testifies about the program's impact on her education and career. She discusses the current epistemic crisis and the importance of preserving rare books and archives.
chapters.title: Jaylen Daniels testifies on Junior Scholars and epistemic crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Good morning, council members and constituents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: My name is Jaylen Daniels, and I'm Jasson's sister.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: And I'm also a proud Junior Scholars alumna here at the Schomburg Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: As native New Yorkers, our favorite thing to do is question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: We all have an insatiable desire to know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Naturally, my New Yorker parents would always tell us the same warning, the people perish for lack of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Though my sister and I attended a great K-12 private school in Manhattan, our truest education and our true wisdom blossomed at home, outside of the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Our parents showed us banned and rare books, manuscripts, documentaries, and artworks often buried by schools and algorithms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: We attended underground debates in church basements, barbershops, and living rooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Where we were exposed to the coolest dissenters often not celebrated in media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: It was a very Harlem Renaissance childhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: My mom came across the Junior Scholars program here at Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Walking over Langston Hughes'ashes and seeing my hero, James Baldwin, revered at the front at age 15 was confirmation that this program would be a sacred experience for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: As a junior scholar, digging through the archives and struggling over the work cultivated my joy for the pursuit of truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: I learned the science of the word, prophetic utterance, and the power of storytelling, the sacred elements that make us human, and that's exactly what the Schomburg did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: It enchanted my humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: The community at Schomburg is its superpower.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: While you learn about the greats, you're surrounded by the greats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Your peers are the next Basquiat's, the next Baldwin's, the next Bell Hooks's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: One of my mentors, an award-winning filmmaker, ended up writing my letter of recommendation to Harvard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: And I work with him on films today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: At Harvard, I studied African American studies and philosophy alongside the greats like Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Skip Gates and Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Cornel West, who treated me as a scholarly peer thanks to the training I received at the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: My thesis, Enemies of the New, Transhumanism, Blackness, and Fleshless Imaginaries, questioned the ontological consequences of a merger between man and machine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: And today we're living in the stakes of this scholarship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: We're in an epistemic crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: More than half of American adults read below a sixth grade level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Our leaders of AI are destroying rare books to feed their models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: And our nation is falling into...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regina Bain
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Okay, well...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: We're reclaiming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: We waited since 10.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: Our nation is falling into mass cognitive resignation as our children swipe on screens rather than pages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: The consequences are dire, and intellectually atrophied people is a people susceptible to deception, groupthink, and fascism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, I left my job to build a rigorous non-AI software in a community

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: where we surface treasures like the one in this building, rare books, and suppress ideas hidden by algorithms in the school system, and we match you with underground thinkers to contest these ideas online and in real life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: My technology maps your epistemic development over time, and we're empowering private collections to become residential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: libraries, the same kind of spaces that powered the Harlem Renaissance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jaylen Daniels
utterances.text: While death lies in the lack of knowledge, it's places like the Schomburg that revitalize life, so we should work to protect it.

chapters.summary: Brent Edwards, professor at Columbia University and director of the Scholars in Residence program at the Schomburg, testifies about hosting 129 fellows. He emphasizes the Schomburg's role as the preeminent repository for African diasporic life and culture.
chapters.title: Brent Edwards testifies on Scholars in Residence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: I'm honored to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: My name is Brent Edwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: I am a professor of English and comparative literature at Columbia University, and I have held two fellowships in the New York Public Library Research Libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
