utterances.text: I was a fellow at the Kuhlman Center for Scholars and Writers at 42nd Street in 2006-2007.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: And I was a fellow here at the Schomburg in the Scholars in Residence program in 1997-98.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: For the past decade, since 2016, I have been, in addition to my job at Columbia, the director of the Scholars in Residence program here at the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: So I'm a Schomburg staff member now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: I counted last night and I have in that capacity personally hosted 129 fellows in our short-term and long-term fellowship program,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: which brings academics, independent researchers and writers, creative writers, novelists, poets and playwrights, journalists, biographers to do research in the unparalleled collections of the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: Without recounting the careers of so many fellows that I've worked with, I'd just say to put it very simply and quickly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: that the Schomburg is the preeminent repository for the documentation of African diasporic life, culture, history, and politics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: It is the foundation of the entire field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: If you work on black studies, you come through the Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: And I would say that more broadly about the research libraries, having done research at Performing Arts and at Schwarzman at 42nd Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: These research libraries are incubators for the best and brightest for everything we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: I also want to underline in closing a message that the previous panel, the previous two panels,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: stressed that although I work with the fellows, with the high-powered academics and creative writers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: As someone who teaches at a university, Columbia, whose gates have been literally locked for the past two years, it's always striking to me to come here in an institution that is open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: And although I work with relatively high-level academics and intellectuals, I'm reminded every day of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: Let me just finish the sentence of the openness of the New York Public Library where I see junior high school kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: kids researching book projects and people doing family genealogy research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brent Edwards
utterances.text: It's a crucial part of what the research libraries represent in the fabric of the city.

chapters.summary: Bill Goldstein, a writer and lifelong New Yorker, testifies about how NYPL's research libraries enabled his books on Virginia Woolf and Larry Kramer. He notes that most New Yorkers don't know these archives are available to the public.
chapters.title: Bill Goldstein testifies on research libraries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: My name is Bill Goldstein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: I'm a writer and a lifelong New Yorker, born in Brooklyn, and now I live in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: I'm here to speak about how vital the research libraries of the New York Public Library have been to me and my work, which would not have been possible without the astounding archival material

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: available at the New York Public Library and the generous professionalism of the librarians and curators who guard and protect the material on paper and in every medium that reveals the past and the roots of the present and the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: I did most of the research for my first book, The World Broke in Two, Virginia Woolf, T.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Eliot, D.H.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Lawrence, and E.M.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Forster, and The Year That Changed Literature, a literary history of the year 1922 at the New York Public Library, and I'm now working on a biography of the writer and AIDS activist Larry Kramer,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: again using many archives at the library, including the papers of the two organizations of which he was a co-founder, Gay Men's Health Crisis and ACT UP, AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: The library has helped make both books possible and preserves history in a way I think most New Yorkers don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: I do a segment about books on NBC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: weekend today in New York, and when The World Broken 2 was published in 2017, I did a segment with the anchor, Pat Battle, about it, and we talked about the research I did at NYPL.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Pat, and presumably most, if not all, viewers, had no idea that Virginia Woolf's diaries, for example, are in the middle of Midtown Manhattan, that the manuscript of Eliot's landmark poem, The Wasteland, is here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: The library preserves the stories of those famous English writers, among others, but also papers preserving the lives and histories of many LGBTQ activists, lesser known than Larry Kramer,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: but as important, some of whom died decades ago of AIDS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: That the library makes it all accessible to the general public is an essential service to the people of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Writers and researchers are then able to make this history known in our small way to the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: I went to New York City public schools and got my PhD in English at the CUNY Graduate Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: The research libraries are another public resource that has made me who I am today as a person and that enables me to write and to make a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: So when Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein
utterances.text: Williams asked the question about how much of the library is used by the general public and then by scholars and researchers, the scholars and researchers are the general public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bill Goldstein

chapters.summary: Key Choi, a retired art dealer pursuing a PhD, testifies about using the New York Public Library and the Vartan Gregorian Center for his research on French artists and Asian art. He emphasizes the importance of open access to knowledge.
chapters.title: Key Choi testifies on research libraries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: My name is Kiel Choi, a proud birthright citizen of Korean heritage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Though a native of New England, I have lived in New York since the early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: This is where I met my wife, where together we raised our son, and where I have over four decades thrived professionally as an art dealer who nurtured a worldwide clientele

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: that comprised preeminent private collections and major museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Frick Collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Subsequent to my retirement in 2016, I had been fervently pursuing a PhD at the Institute of Art History at the University of Zurich.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: My doctoral project explores how French artists engaged with different classes of Asian art that had reached Europe through trade and diplomacy in the mid-18th century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: This research has been facilitated by convenient access to world-renowned research facilities located within a 20-minute subway journey from my co-op apartment on the Upper West Side, the Thomas J.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Watson Library at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the New York Public Library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Together, they afford me infinite opportunities to comprehensively explore not only the critical literature in my field, but also, in many cases, pertinent rare books, prints, drawings, paintings,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: and decorative arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: In addition, the Vartan Gregorian Center for Research in the Humanities, located in the Stephen Schwarzman Building, has offered me not only a commodious space in which to conduct research and to write,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: but also an intellectual home where on a daily basis I encounter and learn from many committed scholars doing important work across a wide range of fields.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Having worked at the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris and the Bodleian Library at Oxford, I can also attest as to how great libraries housed in great historic buildings can also shape one's perspective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: In this respect, the building is exceptional because its place at the heart of this great city signifies how the unfettered pursuit of knowledge is fundamental to the health of our democracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Key Choi
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Chair moves to Puerto Rico Zoom panel; Julio Lopez Varona testifies

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, we are going to go to, is this the last panel of Zoom?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Well, okay, yeah, so we're gonna go to the last panel on Zoom in Puerto Rico, and with that, we'll have Julio, Christian, and Hernales.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And Emma.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Emma.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Emma?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Emma.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I want to say it correctly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Well, good morning, members of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: My name is Julio Lopez Barona.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: I'm from Puerto Rico and have lived through the consequences of austerity measures imposed under the Fiscal Oversight and Management Board and the greed and exploitation of bullish reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Today I'm testifying on behalf of the Commission para Ciudadana para la Auditoría Integral del Crédito Público in support of Resolution

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: 28, calling on Congress to establish a date for ending the board, and Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: 22, supporting New York's legislation to curb predatory debt practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: We are a nonprofit citizen-led organization that conducts independent research on Puerto Rico's public debt and advocates for democratic, rights-based fiscal policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And we have been at the front lines with people like Christian and Christina and others finding the board for more than 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: It's been 10 years after Promesa was created and the Oversight Board,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: and Puerto Rico continues to face austerity measures while all elected officials retain extraordinary control over our budgets and our fiscal policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: During this period, hundreds of public schools have closed, the University of Puerto Rico has faced these cuts, as we heard before, and the island electrical system has been privatized amid

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: resistance, service failures, and blackouts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: This is not a 10-year thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Last Thursday, 400,000 people were without power for about five hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: So this is happening almost every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Meanwhile, hedge funds and other investors have published Puerto Rico's debt at steep discounts, cents on the dollar, have continued pursuing aggressive repayment through the courts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: PREPA, for example, bondholders still are seeking additional payments that could translate into higher electrical bills for people like me, for families, for my mom, and for everybody that lives here, with a power grid that continues to fail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: So the fact that we're paying more doesn't mean that we're getting better service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Puerto Rico's experience is not unique.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: In cases involving Puerto Rico, Argentina, and Greece, some creditors have relied on litigation to extend the capacity they have to litigate and to make more money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: This practice creates incentives that allow for these external players to come in to make more money and to further suffer in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And this is where New York comes to play.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Champerty and related practices can create the incentives that make it even worse for Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: 27 can help address these practices by preventing some really basic financial practices from happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: I want to just make sure that people understand the real human consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Puerto Rico has lost 15% of its population over the last 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Puerto Rico's poverty is at 45% over the poverty line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: So we're talking about how people are living in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Many people are suffering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And also it's important that you understand this is not only a Puerto Rico issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Puerto Rico has 700,000 people that call themselves Puerto Rican living in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And those families are connected to what's happening in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Those are the people that are moving money to Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And those are the people that got like gave homes to Puerto Ricans when Puerto Rico had Hurricane Maria.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: But also you should remember that it's not only Puerto Ricans, it's the rest of the world living in Puerto Rico and in many cases migrating to New York because they cannot sustain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: the impacts that these headphones have had on the island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: With all of that said, we urge the council to pass those resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Puerto Rico should be determined by democratic governance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: We might have a crappy governor, but we still want to make sure that we have a governor that we can hold accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: And financial practices should not allow investors to profit at the expense of community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: People should always come before profits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julio Lopez Varona
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration.

chapters.summary: Cristian E. Martinez, security director of Construyamos Otro Acuerdo, testifies in support of Resolution 28. He describes how the fiscal board has cut pensions and prioritized payments to Wall Street bondholders.
chapters.title: Cristian E. Martinez testifies on Resolution 28

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: We strongly urge the council to pass the resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Construyamos Otro Acuerdo is a community organization dedicated to developing community leadership and strengthening the collective power of communities in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Our mission is to train, support our communities impacted by economy and social challenges so that they can participate in an informed and effective manner in processes that affect their collective well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Our work addresses key issues such as authority, pensions, unfair working conditions, and tax breaks that benefit a few at the expense of the majority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Since its inception, the unelected and undemocratic Junta has put forward an agenda

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: that has prioritized payment to Wall Street over the people of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: COA has seen the impact that Promesa and La Junta had in Puerto Rico for a hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Over the last 10 years, we have seen clear examples of this agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: The board has also overseen and supported the restructuring and privatization of Puerto Rico's electoral system, while Puerto Ricans continue to experience, as Julio mentioned, unreliable service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: and constant blackout.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: During this time, COA membership has felt the impact of these actions and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Our members include thousands of government pension holders who were treated with cuts to their pensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: After years of fighting, we were able to stop the cuts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: However, the debt adjustment process resulted in restrictions of future pensions increases, including eliminating the COLA adjustment,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: including a prohibition on increasing defined benefit pensions payment time expired with the plan of adjustment for a period of 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: While our members struggle, we have seen how Wall Street bondholders, including investors who acquired Puerto Rico debt in the distressed market, have litigated to secure substantial payments under claims.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: In Puerto Rico, debt restructuring bondholders have received significant recoveries, including new bonds and other considerations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: While some claims also insult future payment tied to the performance of Puerto Rico revenues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Those bondholders can receive payment for decades while our right to read struggle to keep up the rising cost of living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: That's why we support Resolution 28.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Because Congress should establish a clear and definite timeline for ending the Financial Oversight and Management Board, La Junta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: We further encourage policymakers to ensure that any transition away from the board includes a transparent public accounting of its

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: action, meaningful participation by the people in Puerto Rico in determining the island's fiscal future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: We respectfully urge the New York City Council to pass this resolution and stand with the people of Puerto Rico in advancing justice for our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: After 10 years of federal fiscal control, Puerto Rico deserves a clear path back to all their accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cristian E. Martinez
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration.

chapters.summary: Eva Prados, executive director of the Puerto Rico Citizen Commission for the Audit of Public Credit, testifies in support of Resolution 28. She discusses the commission's report 'A Lost Decade' and the board's failure to address structural causes of the fiscal crisis.
chapters.title: Eva Prados testifies on Resolution 28

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: My name is Eva Prados, and I'm here as the Executive Director of the Puerto Rico Citizen Commission for the Audit of the Public Credit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: I'm from Puerto Rico, and like millions of residents, I have lived through the consequences of the decision imposed on our island over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: I want to thank Council Member Alexa Viles and the rest of this Council for considering Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: 28, which calls on Congress to establish a specific date for ending the Puerto Rico Financial Oversight and Management Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Ten years after PROMESA imposed the board, Puerto Rico continues to face deep economic and social challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: The board has exercised extraordinary authority over our government, challenged legislation, imposed fiscal policy, and prioritized

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: debt repayment, while essential public services and democratic decision-making have suffered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Our recent report, A Lost Decade, on Maxkin La Junta in Puerto Rico, documents several serious concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Due to time constraints, we submit a summary of this report as part of our registration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: And on our findings, the board's report

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Debt savings do not fully account for billions in cash and additional payments to bondholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Meanwhile, austerity measures have contributed to cuts and privatization of essential services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: And Puerto Rico fiscal crisis has not been solved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Promesa on the board have not addressed the structural causes of Puerto Rico fiscal crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Its emphasis on debt payment, fiscal plans, and balanced budget has not resolved the underlying economic and political condition that contributed to economic stagnation and accumulation of public debt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: After 10 years of fiscal control, we continue to face fragile infrastructure, unreliable essential services, and economic vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Puerto Rico needs democratic decision-making, transparency, and accountability, not indefinite federal control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: We urge the New York City Council to pass Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: 28 and call on the Congress to establish a clear date for ending the board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: The people of Puerto Rico deserve the right to determine their own fiscal and economic future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eva Prados
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Suheili Serrano Marrero, a municipal legislator from Vega Baja, testifies in Spanish in support of Resolutions 28, 372, and 494. She describes the impact of austerity on municipalities and opposes Project Esencia.
chapters.title: Suheili Serrano Marrero testifies in Spanish on resolutions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Suheili.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Buenas tardes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Buenas tardes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Mi nombre es Suheili Serrano Marrero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Comparezco hoy como legisladora municipal del Movimiento Victoria Ciudadana en la legislatura municipal de Vega Baja, Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Para mí, expresar mi apoyo a la resolución 0028 que exige al Congreso de Estados Unidos establecer una fecha de salida

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: para la Junta de Control Fiscal, su impacto negativo en la vida cotidiana en Puerto Rico y en los recursos disponibles que los municipios brindan esencialmente.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Durante la última década, la UPR y los gobiernos municipales han sido los principales afectados por recortes masivos, presupuesto de la Junta de Control Fiscal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Dichos recortes han afectado más a los municipios pequeños y según los estudios de las ligas de ciudades, la Junta ha puesto en riesgo de desaparecer 43 municipios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: En algunos casos, la pérdida de estos recursos llegó a representar hasta un 60% de su Fondo General Municipal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Como consecuencia, cerca de un tercio de la población del país vive en municipios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: sin fondos suficientes para brindar los servicios esenciales básicos como la recogida de basura, mantenimiento de carreteras, parques, transporte e iluminación, por mencionar algunas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: De manera paralela, la Junta impulsó la precarización de las condiciones laborales.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: La privatización de los servicios esenciales y la construcción de proyectos en abierto desafío a un plan de uso de terrenos,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: con el subsiguiente impacto negativo al ambiente natural y la sostenibilidad humana y social.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Con su apuesta fiscal y sus reformas, la Junta ha arriesgado

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: y desplazado a todo un pueblo que cada día se le hace más difícil vivir en Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: También quiero mostrar mi apoyo a la resolución 0372 para la derogación de la ley 22 y luego la ley 60, que ha creado un paraíso fiscal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: para algunos y no para los puertorriqueños, y expresar el bienestar de nuestro país que está pasando escasez y acceso seguro a los servicios públicos más importantes como la agua y la luz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Como residente de Puerto Rico, también exijo mi total oposición al desarrollo de proyectos como Esencia, que solo desplaza a nuestras comunidades para enriquecer a unos pocos, una vez más.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: limitando a nuestro acceso al agua, dañando nuestros recursos naturales y creando ciudades para ricos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Por tanto, apoyo también la resolución 0494, pidiendo no a excedencia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suheili Serrano Marrero
utterances.text: Y libertad de determinación de los puertorriqueños sobre nuestro territorio.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams calls the Brooklyn Public Library panel. Stacey Bell, president of the Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society, testifies about using the Center for Brooklyn History to research her family history and the importance of preserving these records.
chapters.title: Chair calls Brooklyn Public Library panel; Stacey Bell testifies

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Gracias por tu testimonio.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just got a quick lesson.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm not that good.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much for everyone joining us from Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: With that, we'll turn it back to the libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We are going to hear from Brooklyn Public Library, Stacey, Aina, Dominique, Megan, and Yonina.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I believe this is the last library panel, and then we'll go to testimony from, I'm sure, many folks who have been here all morning from 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I see people who are here since 10.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So thank you so much for your patience.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And Megan is from the Schaumburg, but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think she can hang out with the Brooklyn folks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I don't know if people left, but Stacey, Aina, Dominique, Megan, and Yonina.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Do you want us to start without the full panel?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You can start, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Buenas tardes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: My name is Stacey Bell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: I am the president of the Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society, Gene Sampson Scott Greater New York Chapter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: We just call ourselves OGS New York for short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Libraries are more than buildings filled with books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: They are keepers of our collective memory.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Institutions like the Center for Brooklyn History preserve the evidence that connects New Yorkers today to the people who walked the Brooklyn streets 500 years ago, 100 years ago, and 50 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Without these research archives, I wouldn't know about the Pawpaw family,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: a family of African and Lenape descent who had a homestead in Midwood, Brooklyn in the 1850s, or their contemporaries, the Copeland family, who lived on Union Port Road in the Bronx until they were driven away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: During the New York draft riots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: They sought refuge in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: They couldn't return to the Bronx because their land had been taken from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: D-theft and displacement are not new.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: I want to call another name, and this one is personal, Sam Anderson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: In 1898, the Brooklyn Daily Eagle article penned Sam as the last slave of Flatbush.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Sam was born in 1813 and was enslaved by the Lott family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Near what we now know today is Flatbush and Cortellu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: I live in Flatbush, right near Cortellu Road.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: 2025, the Center for Brooklyn History centered Sam Anderson and his descendants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Yes, there are descendants of people who were enslaved in New York City still living in New York City today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: In an exhibit appropriately called Traces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: The visitors who interacted with this exhibit saw evidence of who was enslaved here, what they built, what was taken, and how their lives are connected to ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: We were able to follow up the exhibit with genealogy workshops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Supporting these institutions will make sure the people who we hear before us are not erased from history a second time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ayanna Deleuze, a master's student at CUNY, testifies about visiting the Center for Brooklyn History and learning about its exhibition on the Battle of Brooklyn. She highlights the center's inclusive research library and upcoming exhibition on Puerto Rican Brooklynites.
chapters.title: Ayanna Deleuze testifies on CBH exhibition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: My name is Ayanna Deleuze.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: I was born and raised in Brooklyn, and I'm currently a master's student at the CUNY Graduate Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: This past March, I had the opportunity to visit the Center for Brooklyn History with my public scholarship class to learn about their current exhibition, The Battle of Brooklyn, Fought and Remembered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: During the exhibition tour, our class learned about the work behind curating the exhibition and its storytelling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: The exhibition uses primary sources from their collection to explore how Brooklyn itself was part of a significant turning point in the American Revolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: It also examines how the public memory of the battle has transformed, shaping how Brooklynites understand Brooklyn's revolutionary war past from the 19th and 20th centuries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: My class and I gained valuable insight into the work it takes to curate a historical exhibition for a public audience from all walks of life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: After my class and I toured the exhibition, we were invited to the Ottermer Library to look at their archival materials that didn't make it into the exhibition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: There we learned that their research library is not exclusive to professional readers and academics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: The library offers an inclusive place where anyone can utilize the space and its resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: They welcome all members of the public, whether they want to research aspects of Brooklyn's diverse history or have a quiet place to study.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: Next year, the Center for Brooklyn History will host an exhibition centering the histories of Puerto Rican Brooklynites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: As a third-generation Puerto Rican Brooklynite who is researching the understudied history

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: and culture of South Brooklyn's Puerto Rican community, I was ecstatic to hear this news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: In public history, we have the responsibilities to ourselves and our communities to preserve underrepresented histories and the voices of those who have lived them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: Ultimately, the core of the Center for Brooklyn History's work is a collaborative effort between the institution and the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: Their approach makes Brooklyn histories visible, accessible, and engaging for the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ayanna Deleuze
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dominique Jean-Louis, chief historian at the Center for Brooklyn History, testifies about the urgent need for conservation funding. She notes that some materials, like a rope used in the draft riots, cannot be digitized due to wear and tear.
chapters.title: Dominique Jean-Louis testifies on conservation needs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: My name is Dominique Jean-Louis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: I'm chief historian of the Center for Brooklyn History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: I'll do my best to keep my remarks very brief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: You heard earlier from Roberta Pereira that we're in the business of forever, but I want to underscore that we don't have forever to fulfill our duty to the history of New York City and at the Center for Brooklyn History, specifically Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: When I first began researching Brooklyn in the 1970s and listening to oral history tapes, I remember being reminded that these cassette tapes have a shelf life of 30 to 50 years, and they were reaching the end of their viability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: That was 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: The materials in our collection, we do our best to preserve, but we currently don't have a conservation budget, meaning that even if we had the money to digitize everything in our collection, there are certain items that won't

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: be able to be digitized just because of wear and tear and the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: So our financial needs are not just prevalent, they're urgent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: We don't have the ability to wait forever to be able to expand the access to our collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: And I just want to make one more point about the importance of conservation and the lack of a conservation budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: Stacey just mentioned the New York City draft riots, the largest civil disturbance in United States history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: We hold in our collection an important piece of that history, a rope used to lynch a black man during that collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: We are forced to choose between seeking out private money, grant money, if we're able to get it, or leaving that important piece of history tucked away in storage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: We don't have the ability to share everything we have because of the limitations of that conservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: So our impact is immense, as you've heard, but also the need is also immense, and the need is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: Left to wait, we won't be able to preserve this history for the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dominique Jean-Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks the panel and discusses the recent council bill on the draft riots. She notes the importance of connecting with CBH to mark this dark time in New York City history.
chapters.title: Chair Williams thanks panel and discusses draft riots history

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And as I've said in other panels, please reach out to us and let us know.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I mean, I think the library systems are so large and sometimes the advocacy doesn't get into the nuances, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So it's a pleasure to learn about what the libraries are doing, but also a little alarming that we really didn't have this information prior to this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I guess that's what hearings are for, for people to, for us as members to hear and learn from your institutions and from the public.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We recently passed a bill in the council around the draft riots, so we should definitely connect because we hope that DCLA will do something to mark this dark time in New York City history.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think we have a...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: A tendency to look at all the flowery and nice things that have happened, but we sort of skip over the dark past.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we'd love to connect with you and look forward to working with all of you, especially you all as well.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that during the draft riots, we've all heard of the Weeksville community, but during the draft riots, Brooklyn was a refuge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: It was the place that people went.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Brooklyn was a wilderness at that point, especially mid-Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: So there's so much history there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: We walk those streets and it reminds me to remind people that we're all...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: connected, the people that are going through things today, the people that are seeking refuge in Brooklyn today are connected to those people whose families met those ropes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, and I learned the other day, you just mentioned it, that the draft riots were also happening in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think sometimes we focus on Manhattan, the city, but it did happen in other parts of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So we definitely should connect.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you're not already connected to Regina or Shaquille from my office, who's probably floating around, I would love to connect with you all and continue the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stacey Bell
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams calls the next panel. Minerva Diaz testifies about her exhibition inspired by the song 'Lo Que Le Pasó a Hawaii' and draws parallels to displacement in Puerto Rico and San Juan Hill in Manhattan.
chapters.title: Chair calls next panel; Minerva Diaz testifies on displacement

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, next panel, Madeline, Donald, Nilsa, Aviles, are y'all cousins?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yesenia, Aviles, oh you got a whole bunch of cousins, and Minerva Diaz.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is there a turn here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: However you, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: So I'm just going to get this going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker, Council, thank you for doing this and good seeing you again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: And Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Alvarez, thank you for bringing these three resolutions to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: My name is Minerva Diaz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Me llamo Minerva Diaz, born Minerva Ortiz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I'm going to speak in English because my Spanish is not so great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Okay, so my name is Minerva Diaz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: My mother came from Puerto Rico to Manhattan's Lower East Side with her family when she was 14.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: My siblings and I are first generation born here in the States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I didn't know about Resolution 494 until my cousin, Nelsa, shared it with me a few days ago via text.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: My immediate response was, shall I meet you there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Days earlier, we were here in Harlem celebrating the opening of my latest exhibition, Preciosa, My Mother, Her Island, inspired by the song Lo Que Le Pasó a Hawaii.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I had never heard that song before this year's Super Bowl halftime show.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: The words tore through me, they broke my heart, and I couldn't shake them loose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I understood the emotional depth of the song, but I didn't understand its connection to Hawaii until I began researching the parallels between Hawaii and Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: The loss of land,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: displacement of local communities, and the fear of losing cultural identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Although my mother built her life here in the States, Puerto Rico never stopped being her home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: That is why Resolution 494 resonates so deeply with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: And we don't have to look as far as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Hawaii or Puerto Rico to understand the consequences of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Right here on our own island of Manhattan, we have San Juan Hill, an 18 block black and brown community of approximately 7,000 residents and 800 business

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: that was uprooted in 1958 through eminent domain to build Lincoln Center and Fordham University's Manhattan campus.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: There is currently a traveling exhibition, Afterlives of San Juan Hill, documenting what happened to that community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: It is on view at Fordham University.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: At the museum till October 4th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: I encourage everyone to see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: And I'm gonna end with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Today as we discuss the Project Essencia, the history raises an important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: What have we learned and how do we ensure that voices of existing communities here heard before decisions are made that could permanently change their lives, homes, and identities?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Minerva Diaz
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

chapters.summary: Yesenia Aviles testifies about the need for reliable water, electricity, and affordable housing in Puerto Rico. She opposes construction on public beaches and calls for protecting the environment and communities.
chapters.title: Yesenia Aviles testifies on protecting Puerto Rico

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: My name is Yesenia Villas, a proud Puerto Rican.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: I guess sentimental.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: I'm here today because I love Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: I love the people, and they deserve to come first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Before new projects are thought of being built, our communities deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Okay, deserve the basics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Consistent running water, reliable electricity, safe infrastructure, and affordable homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: People should not be living with interruptions to essential services while large developments are being proposed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: No consistent water for Puerto Ricans, but the government wants to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: I also say no building on public beaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Our beaches are part of Puerto Rico's natural heritage and belong to the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Construction in sensitive coastal areas can damage coral reef, marine life, and the ecosystem that protects our coastline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Coastlines should not be changed to benefit developers and displace the Puerto Rican people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: We must protect Puerto Rico families from being displaced from their homes and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Development should not mean that local people lose access to their land and neighborhoods or beaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: We are not against Puerto Rico improving and prospering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: We are saying that the people and environment must come first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: So today our message is clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Give our community reliable water, electricity, protect public beaches, protect coral reef and ecosystems, protect Puerto Rican families and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: And protect Puerto Rico future generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Our beaches are not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Our communities are not for sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Our future is not for sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Thank you, but no thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Esencia no va.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yesenia Aviles
utterances.text: Las playas son de pueblo.

chapters.summary: Nilsa Aviles, co-founder of Ignite and Rise, testifies about her aunt's anxiety due to unreliable water and electricity in Puerto Rico. She argues that basic services must be reliable before approving massive developments.
chapters.title: Nilsa Aviles testifies on water and electricity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: My name is Nilsa Aviles, co-founder of Ignite and Rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: I am a blessed, I'm blessed because I'm Puerto Rican.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: I am firmly against Essencia and all projects that aren't for the people of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Before we talk about building massive development,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: that will require enormous resources, why don't we take care of the people who are already living there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: There are communities that continue to struggle with unreliable water and electricity that is unreliable for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: That inconsistency and uncertainty affects people's lives and their mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: I want to speak about my aunt that lives in Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Because of the inconsistent light and the inconsistent water, she's been suffering from anxiety, from depression, and this is not...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Something that she used to suffer with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: It's just now that she's just always like nervous about, oh, you know, the water, oh, the electricity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: And I think this is a mind game that they're playing with the Puerto Rican people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: They're trying to break us down little by little, but we're made from strong stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Water is not a luxury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Water is life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: I believe our people should have reliable water consistently for more than two or three years before they even consider

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: a project of that magnitude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: And this is bigger than just water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Puerto Ricans have been fighting to protect our land for generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Today we are still saying this is our land, these are our beaches, these are our mountains, these are our rivers, these are our wetlands, these are our

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: oceans, our turtles, manatees, and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Progress should not come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Progress should not come to the expense of the Puerto Rican people who already live there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Before you approve a billion-dollar project, make sure the people of Puerto Rico have reliable electricity and water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Protect our lands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Esencia no va.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nilsa Aviles
utterances.text: Que viva Puerto Rico.

chapters.summary: Madeline Jackson testifies about how the library system educated her on local history and displacement. She highlights the research libraries' role in providing access to information and calls for expanding resources to Weeksville.
chapters.title: Madeline Jackson testifies on libraries and displacement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Madeline Jackson, and I live on the Lower East Side, and I would be preferred to stay home, but the library system essentially woke me up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: I think I was sleeping most of my life until I learned that there was a space where you can actually come and do presentations and learn about your history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: This is where I live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Most people know about this symbol here where every time there is a rally, people go to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: The gentleman behind that is an African-American gentleman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: I live behind that monument, and I came to be involved in that because of displacement and trying to rally my community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: There was mention of the draft riots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Little did I know after me organizing with my community, learning later, that the block that I stood on to take petitions to keep a building from being built where I live at, which is directly by the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Brooklyn Bridge Prime Real Estate, so I understand perfectly well what the panelists here are speaking of, because we're fighting very hard to keep our saying what we do with our public space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: But draft riots happened there as well, and I learned that history being previewed to the research libraries, which was always so very welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: I've always felt like if I needed...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: It's something I can go to the research libraries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: I've had experience with not only the Schomburg, but the Center for Brooklyn History and the Performing Arts Library, where I also learned about the history of music, black music, and the importance of how it uplifts us and why we, as a people who are so oppressed,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: gravitate to music and how it was used to uplift and bring messages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: And I think it's very important that also one thing that was not mentioned, I also used to belong to ASOLA, which is the Study of African American Life and History.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: You all know these folks as the stewards of Black History Month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: The honor of belonging to that organization was that I had privy to information that ordinary people would not have had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: It is a membership organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: You have to have $100 to belong there, but being a library member,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Having a library card gives me access to those same privileges that I would have had being part of a legacy organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: So I thank you for having this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: It needs to be expanded to Wheatsville.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Wheatsville is not a research institution, but they hold a lot of information that connects the history of our black community, our oppressed community, to there as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Donald Clayton, executive director of the Harlem International Museum of Black History and African Culture, testifies about the museum's 50-year history. He requests city partnership and investment for a permanent home in Harlem.
chapters.title: Donald Clayton testifies on Harlem International Museum

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: And I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to come before you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: My name is Donald Clayton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the Harlem International Museum of Black History and African Culture, HIM.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to present testimony on behalf of an institution that has served Harlem and New York City for more than five decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Founded in 1972 as the Genesis Museum of International Black Culture,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: HIM is a non-profit cultural educational institution chartered by New York State Education Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: From its beginning, the museum's purpose has been to provide history, art, and cultural education through collection, documentation,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: preservation, interpretation, exhibitions, and dissemination of the histories and art achievements of black and African people throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Currently operating on West 126th Street in Harlem, HIM has presented exhibitions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: educational programs, lectures, cultural programs, and heritage experiences that connect the histories of Africa,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: the global black diaspora, with Harlem, New York City, United States, and the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: HIM appeared before the committee today to present its request for New York City, the partnership and investment towards establishing a permanent home for the museum in Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Such a facility would enable HIM to preserve and make public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Accessible, its collection, developed, permanent, and changing exhibition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Expanding educational program for New York City students and families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Were you done?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, you can finish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Before the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: The museum therefore asked the City Council and New York City

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: and New York to consider a long-term public partnership with HIM that could include identifying and appropriating city-owned sites or facility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: in Harlem, providing capital, operating support, and creating a pathway towards the institutional stability necessary for HIM to serve future generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: New York City already maintains a long-standing public-private model through the Department of Cultural Affairs for the cultural institutions operating on city-owned property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: HIM seeks the opportunity to develop the organizational, capital, collection, educational, and facilities framework necessary to participate fully in New York City's cultural infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: A permanent home would allow more than five decades of HIM's cultural stewardship to be transformed into a lasting public resource,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: one capable of preserving, collecting, expanding access to Black and African history, supporting educators and students, strengthening

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Harlem's cultural landscape and welcoming residents and visitors from around the world,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: HIM respectfully asked the council to begin formal dialogue with the museum, the Department of Cultural Affairs, and other appropriate city agencies to examine the feasibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: requirements, and potential pathway for establishing a permanent city-supported home for the Harlem International Museum of Black and African History and Culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donald Clayton
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Williams thanks Donald Clayton and calls the next panel. Jerry Maldonado testifies in support of all four resolutions, connecting Puerto Rico's debt crisis to New York City's own history of austerity.
chapters.title: Chair thanks and calls next panel; Jerry Maldonado testifies

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I don't know if you pre-registered, if we have your contact, but we'd love to connect with you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I still don't see Shaki from my office in the audience, but please, if you could share your information with Regina, that would be amazing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And thank you so much to you for testifying and for being patient and vulnerable and staying with us the last couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Next panel, Gabrielle, Alice, David, oh, Alice.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Jerabel?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I said David already.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: David Galarza, Jarabel Arroyo, Jerry Maldonado, and Jorge Lopez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Jackson
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We said Jorge.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's you?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Whoever wants to start, do your thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Maldonado
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Maldonado
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Maldonado
utterances.text: Hello.
